title: Backup restoration parses unbounded file contents on the client
description: The restore path accepts an arbitrary browser File and reads its complete contents into memory with File.text(), then parses the complete string with JSON.parse(). There is no file-size limit, streaming parser, structural depth limit, or other resource guard in this service. A caller that permits a user-selected or otherwise attacker-supplied backup file can provide a very large or deeply nested JSON document, causing substantial browser memory allocation and main-thread CPU use during decoding/parsing, potentially freezing or crashing the client.

trace.description: The exported restore(backupFile: File) method receives a File from a caller outside this file; the file contents are attacker-controlled if an attacker can induce or supply backup-file selection.
restore reads the entire file via backupFile.text(), with no maximum size check or incremental/streaming processing before materializing its contents as a string.
The full unbounded string is passed to JSON.parse(), which consumes CPU and allocates objects on the browser main thread without a size or nesting-depth limit.

title: Unbounded chat request and streamed-response buffering
description: The chat client accepts an unbounded message array/content payload and opens a streaming response without any request-size, response-size, chunk-count, or stream-duration limit. Every received chunk is retained in the `chunks` array until the async generator yields it. A caller that submits oversized chat content, or induces a very large/long-lived model response, can therefore cause excessive request bandwidth and unbounded browser-memory growth. Backend, proxy, or model-provider limits may mitigate this, but no such control is present in this service.

trace.description: `streamMessages` is an exported service method whose `messages` array and each message's `content` are received from a caller outside this file; neither the number of messages nor content length is constrained here.

The complete caller-supplied message array is POSTed to the chat endpoint with no body-size limit, and the request enables progress-based streaming without a timeout, cancellation mechanism, or response limit.

Each parsed response chunk is appended to the in-memory `chunks` array with no maximum count or total-content cap. A prolonged or high-volume stream can grow client memory until the generator drains it, potentially degrading or crashing the browser tab.

title: Path traversal escapes the static-data directory
description: `loadStaticData` accepts an unconstrained file identifier and constructs a filesystem path by concatenation before normalizing it with `path.resolve`. `path.resolve` normalizes `..` segments but does not enforce that the resulting path remains under `./data/static`. A caller able to influence `file` can supply traversal segments (for example, `../../sensitive-config`) and cause the function to read and parse `data/sensitive-config.yml` or another reachable YAML file outside the intended static-data directory. The `.yml` suffix limits targets to YAML-named files, but does not provide an authorization or directory-containment control. Reachability from an attacker-facing caller is outside this file, but the exported parameter is the unprotected boundary here.

trace.description: Exported `loadStaticData` receives the `file` identifier from its caller; that caller is outside this file, and no allow-list or other restriction is applied at this API boundary.

The caller-controlled identifier is concatenated into a path and passed to `path.resolve`. Resolution collapses traversal segments but does not verify that the final path starts within the intended `./data/static` directory.
The resolved, potentially escaped path is read from the local filesystem. There is no containment or authorization check between path construction and this file-read sink.

title: Password-change credentials transmitted in URL query string
description: The password-change request is explicitly constructed as a GET URL containing the current password and both new-password values in its query string. Query strings are routinely retained in browser history, reverse-proxy and web-server logs, monitoring traces, and potentially Referer headers. Anyone with access to those records can recover the plaintext credentials and use them to authenticate as the affected user. The test's HttpTestingController assertion demonstrates that this request shape is intentional service behavior, rather than merely test input.

trace.description: The test supplies plaintext current and replacement password values to UserService.changePassword; the caller of the actual service is outside this spec file.
The expected outbound request URL embeds current=foo, new=bar, and repeat=bar as URL query parameters for a GET request, exposing password material to URL-retention channels.

title: OAuth bearer token placed in request URL
description: The OAuth bearer access token passed into oauthLogin is expected to be included in the Google userinfo request URL as access_token=at. Bearer tokens in query strings can be captured by client history, HTTP/proxy logs, telemetry, and diagnostic tooling. A party obtaining the token can replay it to the OAuth resource server until it expires. Although this file is a unit test, its request assertion confirms the service's token transport design.

trace.description: The test passes a caller-controlled OAuth access token to UserService.oauthLogin; callers of the real service lie outside this spec file.
The expected userinfo request puts that bearer credential in the access_token query parameter, a URL-based credential transport prone to logging and history disclosure.

title: Unbounded concurrent basket-merge requests
description: Guest-basket merging has no item-count limit, quantity cap, or concurrency control. An attacker can populate the same-origin sessionStorage guestBasket value with many distinct ProductId entries (or drive the public client methods with excessive values), then invoke mergeGuestBasketIntoUserBasket. The service turns every distinct product into a request and submits them simultaneously through forkJoin. This can generate a large burst of reads and writes against the basket APIs and degrade service availability; sessionStorage capacity bounds the payload but does not provide a safe request/concurrency bound.

trace.description: Caller outside this file supplies targetBasketId to the exported mergeGuestBasketIntoUserBasket method; guest basket contents originate from caller-controlled same-origin sessionStorage via getGuestBasketItems().
Every guest item is aggregated into a Map with no maximum number of product entries or maximum aggregate quantity.
Each Map entry is converted into an individual update or create HTTP request, with no batch-size or concurrency limit.
forkJoin subscribes to all generated requests concurrently, enabling a single merge operation to issue an unbounded burst of API calls.

title: Client-controlled basket quantities are merged without a business limit
description: The guest-basket workflow accepts and forwards client-controlled quantities without an upper bound. Although persisted sessionStorage entries are checked for positivity and finiteness, they are not capped; moreover addToGuestBasket directly adds its quantity argument and updateGuestBasketItemQuantity assigns any value above one. During merge, the aggregate is sent as the quantity field in basket-item update/create requests. If the server relies on this client-side workflow rather than independently enforcing stock and per-item limits, an attacker can submit extreme quantities, potentially reserving inventory, corrupting basket totals, or causing expensive downstream processing. The server-side validation cannot be verified from this file.

trace.description: Caller outside this file supplies productId and quantity to the exported addToGuestBasket method.
The supplied quantity is added directly to an existing item or stored in a new item without a finite-value, maximum-quantity, stock, or per-basket limit check.
When merging, quantities for the same product are summed without a maximum aggregate limit.
The unbounded aggregate quantity is forwarded to the basket API in either an update or create request; no server-derived stock or permitted quantity is used by this client workflow.

title: Unlimited client-triggered verdict verification requests
description: The public checkLines handler issues a new vulnerability-verdict request every time it is invoked, with no local debouncing, in-flight request guard, attempt limit, or cooldown. A user can repeatedly trigger the UI handler (or invoke it from browser developer tools) to create arbitrary concurrent requests to the backing verdict service. This file cannot establish whether the server or an upstream proxy rate-limits the endpoint, so the finding is low confidence; absent such server-side controls, this enables request flooding and potentially an answer-oracle brute-force workload against the coding-challenge verification service.

trace.description: The caller is outside this file: checkLines is a public component method expected to be invoked by an attacker-reachable UI action and can also be repeatedly invoked by a user controlling their browser.
Each invocation directly uses the current challenge key and selected-line set; there is no attempt counter, debounce, cooldown, disabled state, or in-flight-request check before submitting.

The component unconditionally subscribes to vulnLinesService.check on every invocation, causing a separate outbound verification request per call. No rate-limiting control is present in this request path.

title: Arbitrary address ID is forwarded to deletion service without ownership binding
description: deleteAddress accepts an address identifier from an external caller/template and forwards it directly to AddressService.del without determining whether the identifier belongs to the current user. A browser user can invoke the component method or manipulate the UI/client state to submit another numeric ID. Because client-side selection is attacker-controlled, the downstream delete API must enforce ownership; no such ownership binding is present on this path. If AddressService.del reaches an API that deletes by ID without server-side owner scoping, this becomes BOLA allowing one authenticated user to delete another user's address.

trace.description: The caller is outside this file: deleteAddress is a public component method that receives a caller-controlled address ID.
The supplied id is used unchanged; there is no comparison with an authenticated identity or with the addresses loaded for the user.
The untrusted identifier is passed to the address deletion service, which is the mutation boundary in this file. Server-side authorization must scope this deletion to the authenticated owner.

title: Unbounded address-list response is loaded and rendered
description: The component requests all addresses and constructs a Material table from the complete response without a page size, maximum result count, or incremental loading. An account able to accumulate many address records can cause a large response to be transferred and retained in storedAddresses and MatTableDataSource, consuming browser memory and rendering CPU. The service/API may impose limits outside this file, but no consumer-side bound is present here.

trace.description: The Angular lifecycle hook is invoked by the framework (caller outside this file) when the address component is initialized.
Initialization invokes load with no pagination or result-size configuration.
load requests the complete address collection through AddressService.get; no limit, page, or cursor is supplied.
Every returned address is retained and used to construct MatTableDataSource, making response size directly determine client memory and table-rendering work.

title: Unbounded chat history and LLM streaming consumption
description: The component accepts arbitrary message content and retains the complete conversation, then sends every prior non-error message to the chat streaming service on each turn. There is no message-size limit, conversation-history/token budget, turn cap, client-enforced rate limit, cancellation/timeout, or cap on streamed output. An attacker can repeatedly submit very large messages or grow a conversation over many turns; each subsequent request retransmits the growing history to the LLM service and the unbounded stream is accumulated in browser memory and persisted. This can drive LLM token/API consumption and degrade client and service availability. Any server-side limits could mitigate this, but no such control is visible in this component.

trace.description: sendMessage receives externally influenced chat content from its caller, which is outside this file; it only rejects an empty value and does not impose a length, token, turn, or rate limit.
The submitted content is appended to the in-memory conversation, and all accumulated non-error messages are mapped into apiMessages without any history-size or token-budget truncation.

The complete unbounded apiMessages array is submitted to ChatService.streamMessages, whose stream is consumed without an output, duration, or chunk limit; returned content is continually appended and later persisted.

title: Stored feedback HTML is trusted without sanitization
description: Feedback comments returned by the API are explicitly marked as trusted HTML. This disables Angular's normal HTML sanitization for text that is conventionally user-supplied feedback. If the administration template renders the resulting SafeHtml (as intended by this bypass), a submitted comment such as `` executes in an administrator's browser when feedback is loaded. The framework's default escaping would otherwise prevent this.

trace.description: The `find()` subscription receives feedback records from an API caller outside this file; `feedback.comment` is API-controlled data and feedback content is potentially supplied by application users.
Each returned feedback object is iterated and its comment is selected for presentation.
`bypassSecurityTrustHtml` explicitly suppresses Angular's HTML sanitizer for the untrusted comment before it is placed into the table data source for template rendering.

title: User email is interpolated into trusted HTML
description: User email values from the user-list API are embedded directly into an HTML string and then marked trusted with `bypassSecurityTrustHtml`. An attacker able to register or modify an email value can break out of the span and inject executable markup, e.g. ``. The active-session conditional only selects a fixed CSS class and does not encode or sanitize the email value.

trace.description: The `find()` subscription receives user records from an API caller outside this file, including each user's `email` field.
The component iterates each API-returned user record before rendering the table.
The email is concatenated into HTML and the whole result is passed to Angular's sanitizer-bypass API, so attacker-controlled email markup is treated as safe HTML.

title: Administration lists load unbounded collections before pagination
description: The component fetches complete user and feedback collections with no visible page size, query limit, or incremental loading, then retains and processes every returned record before applying a client-side paginator. An authenticated user who can create many feedback records (or any party able to cause collection growth) can make an administrator's page request transfer, allocate, and iterate an excessive response. The paginator does not constrain the API response because it is attached only after all records have been loaded.

trace.description: Angular invokes `ngOnInit` when the administration page is entered; this lifecycle entrypoint is triggered by routing/callers outside this file.
Page initialization invokes both collection-loading methods.
The user-list request is issued without any pagination or limit argument.
The feedback-list request is likewise issued without a limit, and each received record is subsequently processed locally.
All received feedback records are provided to `MatTableDataSource`; pagination is only attached afterward, so it cannot limit network, memory, or iteration cost.

title: Unchecked rating count can cause excessive client allocation
description: `times` creates an array proportional to an unchecked caller-provided number. If its argument is ultimately derived from a feedback rating or another API value rendered by the administration template, a very large integer can force substantial allocation or throw a range error while rendering the page. The source and reachability of the argument cannot be confirmed from this TypeScript file, but this method itself contains no upper bound appropriate for a star-rating display.

trace.description: The public component method receives `numberOfTimes` from a caller outside this file, likely a template expression or another component consumer.
The value directly controls `Array(numberOfTimes).fill(...)` without a maximum bound, allocating one element per supplied count.

title: Client-controlled UserId permits feedback attribution to another user
description: The feedback payload treats a client-side UserId form control as authoritative. Although it is initialized from whoAmI(), the control is neither disabled nor integrity-protected, and save() overwrites feedback.UserId with its current value immediately before sending the request. An attacker can alter the form control through browser developer tools or invoke the component method with a modified value to submit feedback attributed to another numeric user ID. The receiving API must derive the user identity from the authenticated session or reject a mismatched UserId; no such enforcement exists in this client-side path.

trace.description: The UserId form control is an externally mutable client-side input surface; its value can be changed by the UI caller or browser-side attacker, despite its initial value being supplied by code elsewhere in this component.

save() copies the mutable control value into the security-relevant feedback.UserId property immediately before submission. There is no comparison to the authenticated whoAmI() identity or other integrity/ownership check on this path.
The complete attacker-modifiable feedback object, including UserId, is sent to FeedbackService for persistence/API processing.

title: Unsanitized feedback text is submitted for persistent display
description: Free-form feedback text is incorporated into a comment field and submitted for persistence without sanitization or a content allow-list. The maximum-length validator limits size but does not prevent markup or script payloads. If feedback comments are subsequently displayed through an HTML-interpreting or sanitizer-bypassing rendering path, an attacker can persist a payload such as an event-handler-based XSS payload for execution in viewers' browsers. The eventual rendering sink and any server-side sanitization are outside this file, so exploitability depends on those downstream controls.

trace.description: The feedback form control accepts caller-provided free-form text. Its only relevant restrictions are required and a 160-character length maximum; neither is HTML/script sanitization.
save() embeds the untrusted feedback text in the comment property without encoding or sanitization before it becomes part of the submitted object.
The constructed comment is passed to FeedbackService.save() for API submission/persistence. Any later rendering sink is outside this file.

title: Client-controlled address ID is used for read and update without ownership validation
description: The edit flow takes an address identifier from the client-controlled route and uses it directly for both address retrieval and update. This component performs no ownership or authorization check before loading the returned address into the form or issuing the PUT. If the AddressService/API does not independently scope these operations to the authenticated user, an authenticated attacker can replace the route's addressId with another user's identifier, view that address, and submit changes to it. Client-side routing cannot serve as an authorization boundary, so authorization must be enforced by the service endpoint.

trace.description: Angular supplies a route ParamMap to this component from a caller/router outside this file; its addressId route parameter is attacker-controllable through navigation to an edit URL.
The untrusted route parameter is copied directly into addressId without format, ownership, or authorization validation.
The same identifier is passed to getById and the returned address is used to populate the editable form; no check establishes that the returned record belongs to the current user.
On save, the route-derived addressId is sent directly to the update operation. There is no per-address authorization check in this component between route input and the mutation request.

title: Unsanitized free-form address content is persisted
description: Free-form address fields supplied through the form are copied directly into a persisted address object and sent to AddressService without sanitization or a content allow-list. Address fields such as fullName, streetAddress, city, and state are conventional display fields and can carry HTML/script payloads. If any later address display uses an unescaped HTML/DOM sink, a payload stored through this flow becomes stored XSS. Angular's normal interpolation is safe, but the rendering sites and any server-side validation are outside this file, so the eventual rendering sink cannot be confirmed here.

trace.description: The save method is invoked by a form submission/event handler whose caller is outside this file; the form-control values originate from user-entered address data.
User-controlled form values, including fullName, streetAddress, city, and state, are assigned verbatim to the address object with no sanitization or character allow-list.
The complete address object containing those values is sent to AddressService for creation/persistence. Any later unescaped rendering sink is outside this file.

title: Address creation requests are issued without client-side abuse controls
description: The component exposes an address-creation operation but contains no throttling, request deduplication, submission lock, or payload-size controls before dispatching writes. An attacker can invoke save repeatedly or call the corresponding API directly to create large numbers of address records, consuming database storage and write capacity. Backend/API-gateway rate limits or body limits could mitigate this, but none are visible in this file.

trace.description: The public save handler is reachable from the address form submission path, whose template caller is outside this file.
The handler builds a new address payload from user-controlled controls and does not enforce a submission lock, rate limit, or aggregate request/payload limit before issuing the request.
Each invocation dispatches an AddressService save request, allowing repeated creation attempts that can consume backend write and storage resources if server-side throttling is absent.

title: Unsanitized exported API data is written as executable HTML
description: The component writes an API-controlled export payload directly into a newly opened same-origin document with document.write(). No HTML sanitization, output encoding, or safe download mechanism is applied. If any field included in the exported user data is attacker-controllable (for example, a profile field or other persisted account data), markup such as an event-handler payload can execute in the new window under the application's origin. This is also unsafe if the export response is tampered with or a backend export encoder returns malicious markup.

trace.description: The dataExport service is invoked and its asynchronous response is received by this component; the HTTP caller/endpoint implementation is outside this file.
The externally returned data.userData value is assigned directly to a component property without type validation, HTML sanitization, or context-specific encoding.

The untrusted userData string is passed to document.write(), which parses it as HTML in a new same-origin window. Attacker-controlled HTML/event-handler markup in the response can therefore execute script.

title: Client-controlled localStorage bypasses repeated-export CAPTCHA gate
description: The CAPTCHA requirement intended to slow repeated data exports is decided entirely by browser-controlled state. An attacker can clear or overwrite localStorage.lstdtxprt (or invoke save after changing component state) so needCaptcha() leaves presenceOfCaptcha false. save() then omits the CAPTCHA answer and submits the export request. Consequently, the client-side CAPTCHA cannot reliably restrict repeated export generation; if the service does not independently require and rate-limit CAPTCHA validation, this enables automated repeated export requests and resource consumption.

trace.description: The CAPTCHA timing state is read from localStorage, which is fully writable by the user and can be deleted or set to an old timestamp through browser developer tools or script execution.
Only a timestamp less than five minutes old enables presenceOfCaptcha. A manipulated or absent value causes this conditional CAPTCHA gate to be skipped.

save() includes a CAPTCHA answer only when the browser-controlled presenceOfCaptcha flag is true; therefore an attacker can submit an export request without the intended repeated-export CAPTCHA proof.

The request is sent to the data export service without any local rate limit or server-verifiable proof enforced by this component. Repeated requests can repeatedly invoke export generation unless the unseen backend supplies independent controls.

title: Complaint ownership is supplied in a client-controlled UserId field
description: The complaint payload includes the ownership-bearing UserId relationship as a mutable client-side property. Although it is initially populated from whoAmI, an attacker can modify the in-memory object or forge the POST body and submit a different UserId. The client does not have authority to decide the user relationship of a complaint; the API must derive it from the authenticated token or strictly reject mismatches. If POST /api/Complaints persists this body as sent, an attacker can create complaints attributed to another account, corrupting ownership/audit data and potentially impersonating that user in support workflows.

trace.description: The save() method is invoked from the complaint UI; the event caller is outside this file and can be driven by an authenticated browser user.
The component stores the authenticated user's id in complaint.UserId, a normal mutable JavaScript object property that a requester can alter before submission or replace in the resulting HTTP body.

The complete complaint object, including its caller-controlled UserId property, is passed to ComplaintService.save for transmission to the complaints API. No local invariant removes this property or re-derives it from a trusted server-side identity.

title: File-upload size restriction is only client-side and bypassable
description: The apparent 100,000-byte upload limit is enforced solely by the Angular FileUploader configuration. A requester can bypass this browser-side filter by modifying the client or POSTing directly to /file-upload, so this code does not bound the size or number of requests received by the upload service. This is particularly concerning because the same client intentionally permits ZIP uploads: a small compressed ZIP can expand to consume disproportionate server disk, memory, or CPU if the server processes it. Server-side request-size, archive-expansion, and rate limits are required; their presence cannot be confirmed from this file.

trace.description: A user-selected file reaches the uploader through the onAfterAddingFile callback; the file selection originates outside this file in the browser UI.

The only visible size restriction is FileUploader.maxFileSize, a JavaScript-side filter. The uploader also accepts compressed ZIP MIME types, for which compressed file size does not limit decompressed resource usage.
The selected file is uploaded to the server endpoint when upload() is invoked. Direct requests to that endpoint need not execute the client-side maxFileSize filter.

title: Unbounded image file is loaded into browser memory
description: The image-picker handler accepts a user-selected File with no size limit and immediately reads the entire file as a base64 data URL. MIME validation is configured on the form control, but it does not impose a byte-length limit. A very large image (or a file claiming an accepted image MIME type) causes FileReader to load the full contents into browser memory and create an expanded base64 representation, which can freeze or crash the client tab. The same unbounded file is subsequently retained in the form and may be submitted to the upload service.

trace.description: The caller is outside this file: a user-controlled file-selection event is received by the onImagePicked UI handler.
The handler obtains the selected File directly from the input and stores it in the form. No maximum file size, dimensions, count, or other resource bound is checked before processing.
FileReader reads the entire attacker-selected file as a data URL. This allocates memory for the input and a larger encoded string without a size cap, enabling client-side memory exhaustion.

title: Unvalidated review text is submitted for persistence
description: The review submission handler accepts arbitrary textarea content and sends it unchanged to the review-creation service. The only apparent length control is a reactive FormControl declared at line 49, but addReview reads directly from the supplied HTMLTextAreaElement and does not check that control or perform sanitization/encoding. Thus markup such as can be submitted and persisted if the service stores the supplied message. A later review rendering location outside this file must safely context-encode the stored value; otherwise this is stored XSS affecting users who view the product reviews.

The handler copies textPut.value verbatim into the review message. The declared 160-character FormControl validator at line 49 is not consulted here, and no sanitization, encoding, or length check is applied.

The unvalidated message is passed to ProductReviewService.create for server-side persistence. The persistence and eventual rendering sinks are outside this file; this permits stored markup/script injection if a downstream review renderer uses an unsafe context, and also allows arbitrarily large review bodies to reach the service absent server-side request/body limits.

title: Client-controlled basket ID can target another basket's item update
description: The component treats the browser-writable sessionStorage `bid` value as the authenticated user's basket identifier. A user can modify this value in DevTools and cause the component to fetch a basket chosen by ID; if the returned basket contains the selected product, it then updates the returned BasketItem ID without any ownership or identity validation in this client flow. Client-side `isLoggedIn()` only distinguishes guest behavior and does not bind the basket or basket item to the current account. Server-side authorization must ultimately prevent this, but this code provides no trustworthy identifier binding and directly enables an IDOR request sequence.

trace.description: The `addToBasket` method is invoked by a caller outside this file; for logged-in users it begins a basket mutation workflow.
The component reads `bid` from sessionStorage, a value under the browser user's control, and converts it to the basket ID to retrieve. No binding to the authenticated user is performed.
The basket returned for that attacker-selected ID supplies a BasketItem ID, which is used as the target of the subsequent mutation.

The component sends a quantity update for the selected BasketItem ID without verifying that the basket/item belongs to the logged-in user. An attacker who changes `bid` to a victim basket ID can attempt to alter a matching item in that basket unless the API independently rejects the request.

title: Client-controlled BasketId is submitted when creating basket items
description: When the attacker-selected basket does not already contain the selected product, the component sends a create request whose `BasketId` is copied directly from browser sessionStorage. Since sessionStorage is mutable by the attacker, this lets a user submit basket-item creation requests for arbitrary basket IDs rather than a basket identity derived by a trusted server-side session. This violates the business rule that a user may only add products to their own basket unless the receiving API enforces ownership independently.

trace.description: The `addToBasket` method is invoked by a caller outside this file and accepts the product ID to add.
The method retrieves the basket based on the mutable sessionStorage `bid` value; a browser user can replace this value with another basket ID.
If the retrieved basket lacks the requested product, execution enters the create-item branch rather than establishing that this is the current user's basket.
The request payload explicitly assigns `BasketId` from attacker-modifiable sessionStorage and submits it to the basket-item creation service, with no ownership validation in this file.

title: Payment method submission bypasses client-side validation
description: The component defines client-side validators for payment-card fields, but save() never checks the controls' validity before building and submitting the card. A user can invoke the method or manipulate the form controls through the browser and submit missing, non-numeric, out-of-range, or otherwise invalid values despite the validators. The payment API must independently validate and reject these values; if it relies on this component's validation, malformed payment methods can be persisted and used in downstream checkout workflows.

trace.description: User-controlled values arrive through Angular form controls bound by the caller/template outside this file; save() reads those controls without first requiring that they are valid.

The raw form-control values, including card number and expiry fields, are copied into the request object. Although validators are configured at lines 40-44, no code in save() tests valid/invalid status before this propagation.

The assembled unvalidated card object is submitted to PaymentService.save(). This client-side workflow permits validation bypass unless the API independently enforces card-field validity and business rules.

title: Checkout submits mutable client-side coupon details protected only by Base64 encoding
description: The checkout request carries coupon details from browser-controlled sessionStorage and merely Base64-encodes them with btoa(). Base64 is reversible encoding, not an integrity/authenticity mechanism. An attacker can overwrite couponDetails in DevTools with an attacker-crafted serialized coupon/discount object, Base64-encode it, and submit checkout. If the checkout service accepts the client-provided coupon data rather than independently resolving and validating the coupon and its discount server-side, the attacker can obtain an unauthorized discount. The adjacent client-side computation of couponDiscount likewise shows that promotional values are sourced from mutable browser state. Financial discount eligibility and amount must be derived or cryptographically authenticated by the server, not trusted from sessionStorage.

trace.description: The component receives couponDetails from sessionStorage at checkout time. sessionStorage is writable by the user in the browser, so this value is attacker-controlled; the original writer/caller is outside this file.

The same checkout expression passes the attacker-controlled coupon details through btoa(). This transforms the value but provides neither a signature nor any other integrity protection, so an attacker can create a corresponding encoded value for arbitrary contents.

basketService.checkout sends the encoded, client-selected coupon data along with the basket ID and order details to the order-processing path. No server-derived coupon validation or integrity check is present in this component before the financial checkout sink.

title: Browser-controlled basket ID is used without ownership binding
description: The authenticated-basket lookup uses the basket ID read from browser-controlled sessionStorage and sends it directly to BasketService.find(). This component performs no binding of that ID to the authenticated user returned by whoAmI(), nor any ownership/authorization check before displaying the returned basket's products, quantities, and totals. A user can modify sessionStorage.bid to another numeric basket ID and reload; if the service endpoint does not independently scope the lookup to the authenticated principal, this becomes an IDOR/BOLA disclosure of another user's basket. Server-side authorization must be confirmed in BasketService/the API, but the client-side authorization decision is absent here.

trace.description: The caller is outside this file: load() receives the selected basket identifier from browser-controlled sessionStorage via sessionStorage.getItem('bid').
The untrusted basket ID is passed directly to basketService.find() and the returned basket is used; no comparison to the current user or per-basket ownership check occurs in this component.

title: Unbounded concurrent product requests for guest basket items
description: Guest-basket loading creates one product HTTP request per item and submits all requests concurrently through forkJoin(), with no maximum item count, batching, concurrency limit, or cancellation. Guest basket contents are client-controlled through the basket service/local storage. An attacker can populate the guest basket with a very large number of entries and invoke load(), causing large in-browser allocations and a burst of product requests against the backend. This can degrade the client and amplify traffic to the product endpoint; service-side throttling may mitigate the backend impact but is not present in this code path.

trace.description: The caller is outside this file: loadGuestBasket() obtains the guest item collection from BasketService, whose contents are client-side guest-basket state.
Every guest item is mapped to an individual product request, with no local cap on guestBasketItems or concurrency control.
forkJoin subscribes to all generated product requests at once, allowing an arbitrarily large guest item collection to produce an unbounded concurrent request burst and result aggregation.

title: OAuth callback lacks state validation and permits login CSRF
description: The OAuth callback accepts any access_token present in the redirect fragment but never validates an OAuth state value (or another request-to-callback binding) before establishing a local session. An attacker can obtain a valid OAuth access token for the attacker's own account and cause a victim to visit the OAuth callback URL with that token in its fragment. The application will exchange it for the attacker's profile and store a session token in the victim's browser, producing OAuth/login CSRF: the victim unknowingly acts in the attacker's account. Provider-side validation of the bearer token does not mitigate this because the attacker token is valid; the missing control is correlation to an authorization request initiated by that browser.

trace.description: The OAuth component receives callback data from an external caller/route outside this file through ActivatedRoute snapshot data and treats the fragment as callback parameters.

The fragment is split into arbitrary key/value pairs and returned directly. Although a state parameter could be present, no state/nonce is generated, retained, compared, or otherwise validated anywhere in this callback flow.
The unbound access_token is submitted to oauthLogin, allowing any valid provider token supplied in the callback to select the profile used by this browser.
After the resulting profile is logged in, the application installs the returned authentication token and thereby commits the attacker-selected authenticated identity to the victim browser.

title: OAuth accounts receive passwords derived predictably from their email
description: OAuth-created accounts are assigned a deterministic, reversible password: Base64 of the email address reversed. Base64 is encoding rather than a password-generation or hashing mechanism, and an account email is commonly known or discoverable. An attacker who knows an OAuth user's email can compute this exact password and replay the same login request payload (including the client-controlled oauth flag) to authenticate as that user. The error path after registration also intentionally invokes login, so both newly created and already-existing OAuth accounts proceed with this predictable credential.

trace.description: The component receives an externally sourced OAuth profile after oauthLogin; the OAuth response/caller is outside this file, and profile.email becomes the account identifier used by this flow.
The password is derived solely by reversing profile.email and applying btoa, both deterministic and trivially reversible operations.
This predictable value is persisted as the password when the OAuth user account is saved.
The same predictable value is submitted to the login operation to obtain an authenticated session; an attacker knowing the email can construct the same credential.

title: Bearer authentication token is exposed to JavaScript storage
description: The authentication bearer token is deliberately persisted in localStorage, where every script executing in the application origin can read and exfiltrate it. This includes any successful same-origin XSS, compromised analytics/plugin script, or other script execution defect; token theft remains usable until expiry. The component additionally writes the token using a JavaScript cookie API, which cannot provide HttpOnly protection. No HttpOnly, non-script-readable session mechanism is used in this file.

trace.description: The successful authentication callback receives the bearer authentication.token from the login service.
The bearer token is written to localStorage, a script-readable persistence store, exposing it to any JavaScript that gains execution in this origin.

title: Wallet credit amount is trusted from attacker-modifiable session storage
description: The wallet top-up amount and payment identifier are treated as trusted browser state. A caller can navigate to the wallet payment mode and modify sessionStorage.walletTotal (or invoke the component method through the browser) before choosePayment sends the value as the balance to credit. There is no server-derived amount, payment-provider confirmation, or client-side bounds/positivity check in this payment flow. If the wallet endpoint honors the submitted balance, an attacker can credit an arbitrary wallet amount while supplying an arbitrary or absent paymentId, creating a direct financial-integrity and workflow-bypass risk. The endpoint's server-side validation is outside this file, so it cannot be confirmed here.

trace.description: The payment component receives the route-controlled entity mode through ActivatedRoute; the route caller is outside this file and an attacker can select the wallet branch by navigating to the corresponding payment route.

For wallet mode, the component obtains totalPrice directly from sessionStorage.walletTotal. sessionStorage is wholly controlled by code running in the user's browser and can be altered with developer tools before payment submission.
The payment identifier is likewise mutable component state set from an id supplied to getMessage, with no verification in this component that it represents a completed or matching payment.

The component submits the attacker-controlled totalPrice as the balance to walletService.put, together with paymentId, thereby making the client-controlled amount part of the wallet-credit request rather than deriving or confirming it at a trusted payment authority.

title: Coupon eligibility and discount amount rely on client-controlled time and storage
description: Campaign-coupon eligibility and the resulting discount are enforced entirely in the browser. The component derives the qualifying date from the client clock, accepts a matching campaign, and persists the discount in sessionStorage. An attacker can change the local clock, edit couponDiscount directly, or invoke showConfirmation from browser developer tools. initTotal then calculates the payable cart total with that browser-controlled discount. This component contains no trusted confirmation of campaign eligibility or discount amount before proceeding to checkout. Whether the subsequent order-processing endpoint re-derives and validates the price is outside this file; if it consumes this state or the derived amount, the attacker can obtain an unauthorized or arbitrary discount.

trace.description: The externally triggered applyCoupon UI handler receives the coupon value from the form control; the template caller is outside this file.
The campaign validity decision uses new Date() and a locally calculated timezone offset, so the eligibility check is based on an attacker-controlled browser clock rather than a trusted server time.
On a locally accepted campaign, the component passes the fixed campaign discount to showConfirmation without calling a server-side coupon-validation service.
showConfirmation persists the discount in attacker-modifiable sessionStorage, and initTotal subsequently subtracts couponDiscount from the cart total used by the payment workflow.

title: Unbounded user-controlled Solidity compilation can exhaust browser resources
description: The component accepts an arbitrary Solidity source string and submits it directly to the in-browser Solidity compiler without any source-size, complexity, execution-time, or cancellation limit. An attacker who can supply/paste source into the editor can use deliberately pathological or very large Solidity input to drive expensive parsing/compilation and potentially exhaust browser CPU or memory, freezing the sandbox tab. This is client-side availability impact rather than server-side service exhaustion.

trace.description: compileAndFetchContracts receives the Solidity source as its code parameter; its caller is outside this file (normally the editor/template interaction).
The supplied source is copied verbatim into compilerInput.contractBody with no maximum length, complexity validation, timeout, or cancellation control.
solidityCompiler is invoked on the unbounded attacker-controlled compilation unit, an operation capable of substantial CPU and memory use for adversarial inputs.

title: Runtime Solidity compiler download lacks visible artifact integrity verification
description: Compiler JavaScript is selected by filename but fetched at runtime from a third-party CDN URL, with no visible cryptographic integrity verification (such as a pinned content hash or signed compiler artifact) before handing it to solidity-browser-compiler. HTTPS protects transport but does not establish the integrity of a compromised CDN/origin or substituted release artifact. Since Solidity compilers are JavaScript/WASM-like executable tooling loaded into the application context, compromise of the fetched compiler can compromise the sandbox's browser-origin execution and alter compilation results.

trace.description: The component selects a compiler release filename from a static version-to-filename mapping.
It constructs a remote compiler URL at binaries.soliditylang.org from that filename; no hash, signature, or other independently verified integrity value is included in compilerInput.
The remote compiler artifact is handed to solidityCompiler for retrieval/loading, with no integrity-verification step visible before use.

title: Successful account registrations are not security-audit logged
description: Successful account creation is handled entirely in the browser and only results in navigation plus a snackbar notification. No audit/security logging call records the account-creation event, its outcome, or a correlation identifier. The only error handling in this component is console logging, which is local to the registering user's browser and cannot support server-side detection or investigation of mass registrations or registration abuse.

trace.description: The save() handler is invoked by the registration form; the template/caller is outside this file, and its form values are used to initiate account registration.
The handler submits the new-user payload to UserService, initiating the account-creation operation.
After the user and security answer are created, the code only navigates and displays a snackbar. There is no audit-log or telemetry call for this security-relevant account-creation event.

title: Unbounded recursive filesystem scan and file reads
description: The exported recursive scanner accepts a caller-supplied list of filesystem paths and recursively enumerates every directory entry, reads each encountered file in full, and retains matching file contents in memory. It has no maximum input-path count, recursion depth, directory-entry count, file-size limit, traversal timeout, or cancellation mechanism. If an attacker-facing caller passes an attacker-controlled path (or a path resolving to a large accessible tree), a request can force extensive disk I/O and memory allocation, degrading the service. The internal getCodeChallenges caller uses fixed paths, but the exported scanner itself provides no resource guard if reused by a route or other external-input consumer.

trace.description: The exported findFilesWithCodeChallenges function receives its paths parameter from a caller outside this file; it does not establish a bound or trust requirement for the supplied path list.
Each supplied path is traversed recursively. Directory contents are obtained wholesale, with no cap on entries or recursion depth.
All names returned by readdir are converted into child paths and recursively passed back into the same scanner, allowing a supplied root to expand into an arbitrarily large filesystem tree.
Each non-directory file is read completely as UTF-8 without a size limit; matching contents are subsequently retained in the returned array, consuming disk I/O and process memory.

title: Client-controlled user and address ownership fields are submitted in recycling requests
description: The component constructs the recycling API payload as a mutable client-side object and includes security-sensitive relationship fields (`UserId` and `AddressId`). Although `UserId` is initially populated from `whoAmI`, neither it nor the address identifier is protected from client-side modification, and `save()` forwards the entire object to the API without an allow-list or a local ownership relationship check. An attacker controlling their browser can alter `recycle.UserId` and/or trigger `getMessage()` with another address ID before submitting. If the POST /api/Recycles handler persists these supplied fields rather than deriving the user from the authenticated session and verifying address ownership, this permits creation of recycling requests for another user or against another user's address.

trace.description: `save()` is invoked from the component template/caller outside this file; because it operates on mutable browser-side component state, an attacker can invoke it after altering that state through browser developer tools or a forged UI interaction.

The caller-supplied address identifier received by `getMessage(id)` is assigned directly to `addressId`, then copied into the outbound `recycle.AddressId` property. The previously initialized `recycle.UserId` is retained in the same mutable object; there is no allow-list, immutable ownership binding, or check that the selected address belongs to the current user.

The complete mutable `recycle` object, including `UserId` and `AddressId`, is sent to `RecycleService.save()`. This component does not derive ownership at the submission boundary or restrict the properties that reach the API; server-side enforcement is required but cannot be confirmed from this file.

title: Recycling quantity constraints are bypassable because submission does not enforce form validity
description: The intended recycling quantity bounds are only represented by client-side Angular validators. `save()` reads the raw control value and submits it without checking control validity, so a caller can invoke `save()` programmatically or alter form state to submit a quantity below 10, above 1000, non-numeric, or otherwise invalid. The date and pickup state are likewise copied from client-controlled controls. If the API relies on this UI validation, requests can bypass the business rule and create invalid recycling/pickup operations; validation and any resulting pickup allocation must be re-established server-side.

trace.description: `save()` is a browser-invocable submission handler called by the template/caller outside this file. A malicious client can invoke it directly regardless of UI button state or manipulate its form controls before invocation.

The only visible quantity bounds are Angular client-side validators requiring a value from 10 to 1000. These validators do not prevent a programmatic caller from changing the control value or invoking submission while invalid.
The handler copies the raw quantity value into the request object without checking `recycleQuantityControl.valid`, without revalidating its range/type, and without rejecting invalid form state.

The unvalidated request object is submitted to the recycling API. Whether the API independently enforces the quantity rule is outside this file, but this client component cannot enforce a security-relevant operational constraint.

title: Wallet address is accepted as identity without signature-based ownership proof
description: The component treats the account string returned by an injected wallet provider as proof of wallet ownership and submits it to the application service, but it never requests or verifies a nonce-bound signature. A browser client is not a trust boundary: a caller can alter component state, invoke the service request directly, or supply a malicious/instrumented injected provider that reports an arbitrary account. If the walletAddressSend endpoint uses this request to associate an account, unlock wallet functionality, or award the mint-related success state, an attacker can impersonate another wallet address. Wallet identity must be established server-side by issuing a short-lived challenge and verifying a signature from the claimed address before creating an authenticated association or granting wallet-dependent actions.

trace.description: The Angular lifecycle invokes handleAuth from outside this file; this begins the wallet-authentication flow.

The component obtains a connection result from an externally injected EIP-1193 wallet connector. The returned account is an asserted address, not a cryptographic proof that the application has verified.

The asserted provider account is stored and sent to walletAddressSend without any challenge creation, personal_sign/signTypedData request, signature transmission, or signature verification in this flow.

title: Persistent chain-change listeners enable repeated authentication and request amplification
description: Each component initialization registers a new chainChanged listener on the global injected provider, but the component does not implement OnDestroy or remove the listener. Navigating away and back can leave stale component instances reachable through their bound handlers. A subsequent chain change invokes handleAuth once per retained listener, each invocation disconnects/reconnects and performs wallet/RPC activity and a walletAddressSend request. A malicious or compromised provider can also emit chainChanged repeatedly. This permits unbounded client-side work and unnecessary requests to dependent services as components accumulate.

trace.description: Angular calls ngOnInit from outside this file whenever a WalletWeb3Component instance is initialized.
ngOnInit registers a bound listener on the global wallet provider. No corresponding listener removal or component destruction cleanup is present in this file.

Every retained listener invokes handleAuth, which issues wallet connection activity and then sends a walletAddressSend request; accumulated listeners multiply these operations for one chainChanged event.

title: Admin-login gate trusts an unverified JWT decoded from localStorage
description: waitForAdminLogIn treats the unsigned, attacker-writable contents of localStorage as authoritative for whether an administrator has logged in. jwtDecode only decodes a JWT; it does not validate its signature, issuer, expiration, or authenticity. A user can set localStorage.token to a syntactically valid JWT payload such as {"data":{"role":"admin"}}, causing this helper to return without a genuine administrator session. This directly bypasses the helper's admin-login workflow gate. The visible code does not show a server-side privileged request, so impact is limited to any client-side instructor flow that relies on this helper; server-side authorization must not rely on this result.

trace.description: The exported waitForAdminLogIn helper is callable by code outside this file and is responsible for deciding when the client-side admin-login condition has been satisfied.
The helper reads token from localStorage, a browser-controlled storage location that a user can modify through developer tools or any script running in the origin.
The token string is passed directly to jwtDecode. This operation parses claims but performs no signature or other authenticity verification.
The decoded, unverified data.role claim is used as the identity/role decision: supplying role "admin" ends the wait and signals that the admin-login prerequisite is met.

title: Input-wait helper polls indefinitely without timeout or cancellation
description: The exported wait helper can create a polling task that has no timeout, cancellation mechanism, maximum retry count, or cleanup path. If caller-provided expected input never occurs, the returned callback retains an infinite 100 ms timer loop. If a caller can cause many such tutorial waits to be started (for example through repeated triggering of client-controlled lesson state), this can accumulate timers and DOM reads and degrade the browser tab. Reachability from an attacker-controlled application entrypoint is not visible in this file, so this is a low-confidence client-side resource-consumption finding.

trace.description: waitForInputToHaveValue accepts the selector and expected value from a caller outside this file and returns an asynchronous wait callback.
The supplied expected value controls whether the loop's completion condition can ever become true.
When the condition is not met, execution loops forever and schedules another timer every 100 ms, with no bound or cancellation path.

title: Unvalidated URL is fetched by exported domain-reachability check
description: The exported reachability helper accepts an arbitrary URL and passes it directly to the server-side HTTP client. It performs no URL parsing, scheme restriction, origin allow-listing, or resolved-IP/private-network validation. If a caller outside this file supplies or can influence `domain` (including through a runtime configuration override), it can cause the application host to request loopback/private addresses, cloud metadata services, or an attacker-controlled URL which redirects to such services. The five-second timeout limits request duration but does not restrict the destination, and standard fetch redirect behavior can make redirect-based bypasses relevant.

trace.description: Caller is outside this file: the exported `checkIfDomainReachable` function receives a caller-controlled or externally configured `domain` string.
The supplied URL is sent directly to the server-side `fetch` client without validation of its scheme, parsed origin, redirect target, or whether DNS resolves to a private/internal address.

title: LLM model availability check fetches caller-supplied API URL
description: The exported LLM model check constructs a request target from an unvalidated `llmApiUrl` parameter and sends a server-side request to it. The startup path obtains this value from configuration, but this exported helper has no local guarantee that other callers cannot supply an arbitrary URL. A caller able to influence the value can target internal HTTP services; appending `/models` does not prevent access to an internal service endpoint or an attacker-controlled endpoint that redirects the request. No parsed-origin allow-list or private-address validation is applied.

trace.description: Caller is outside this file: exported `checkIfLlmModelAvailable` accepts the LLM API base URL as a string parameter. The startup caller passes configuration at line 84, but the helper itself accepts arbitrary values.
The base URL is interpolated into a `/models` endpoint and fetched without URL/origin validation or network-address restrictions.

title: LLM availability probe parses an unbounded remote JSON response
description: The LLM model check deserializes the entire HTTP response body using `response.json()` with no response-size cap, streaming limit, or content-length enforcement. The timeout limits elapsed time to five seconds, but an attacker-controlled endpoint (or an internal endpoint reached through the unvalidated URL) can return a very large JSON response quickly enough to cause excessive memory allocation and CPU spent parsing it. The subsequent mapping over all returned models adds further linear memory/CPU work. Exploitability depends on an external caller or configuration path being able to select the LLM URL, which cannot be confirmed from this file.

trace.description: Caller is outside this file: exported `checkIfLlmModelAvailable` receives the URL of the LLM service to probe.
The function requests the remote `/models` resource; only a time limit is supplied, with no response-body size limit.
The complete remote response is parsed as JSON without bounding its size or number of model entries, allowing a selected endpoint to drive memory and parsing consumption.

title: Unauthenticated endpoint discloses the complete application configuration
description: The handler behind the unauthenticated `GET /rest/admin/application-configuration` route returns a clone of the complete server configuration to every caller. It removes only `application.chatBot.llmApiUrl`, leaving every other present and future configuration property exposed. The handler makes no authentication, role, or authorization decision, despite exposing an admin-named configuration endpoint. An unauthenticated attacker can request the route directly to obtain deployment, feature, integration, and security-relevant configuration data; any secret or internal setting added outside the single deny-listed property is automatically disclosed. Accesses are also not recorded, preventing detection or investigation of configuration harvesting.

trace.description: The exported handler receives an HTTP request from a caller outside this file. The registered GET route has no authentication or authorization middleware, and the handler does not inspect the request identity or enforce an administrative role.
The handler clones the entire effective `config` object rather than constructing an explicit public allow-list of configuration fields.
Only one nested property is removed. All other configuration values, including future sensitive fields, remain in `safeConfig`.
The complete remaining configuration is serialized into the HTTP response. This path has no access control check and emits no audit log for this security-relevant configuration disclosure.

title: Unauthenticated admin endpoint exposes application version
description: The unauthenticated GET /rest/admin/application-version route invokes this handler and returns the precise application version whenever application.showVersionNumber is enabled. This exposes deployment/version fingerprinting information through an admin-namespaced endpoint, enabling attackers to select exploits for known version-specific vulnerabilities. The route has no authentication middleware, and this handler performs no authorization check; whether the exposure occurs depends on the referenced configuration value, which is not visible in this file.

trace.description: The exported handler factory is reached by the externally callable route; its caller and route registration are outside this file. The supplied route is unauthenticated.
The returned route handler emits a JSON response containing utils.version() when application.showVersionNumber is enabled, without any access restriction.

title: Unvalidated URL download enables SSRF and unbounded response buffering
description: downloadToFile accepts a caller-supplied URL and passes it directly to the download HTTP client without parsing the URL or enforcing an origin, protocol, resolved-IP, or private-network allow-list. A reachable caller that forwards a request URL can make the server request loopback/private services or cloud metadata endpoints, then persist the returned data. The same operation buffers the entire response in memory before writing it, with no response-size cap, timeout, or request throttling visible in this utility, so an attacker-controlled server can return an oversized body and exhaust process memory.

trace.description: The exported downloadToFile function receives url from its caller; callers are outside this file and this parameter has no local trust boundary or validation.

The supplied URL is passed unchanged to download(). No parsed-origin comparison, scheme restriction, private-address rejection, response-size limit, or timeout is applied here; download resolves and retrieves the caller-selected destination into an in-memory data buffer.

title: Unconstrained download destination permits arbitrary file overwrite
description: downloadToFile also accepts the destination path as an unconstrained parameter and synchronously writes downloaded bytes to that path. If any request-facing caller supplies or derives dest from attacker input, path traversal or absolute paths allow overwriting application files, configuration, or other writable files. This file contains no canonicalization, base-directory containment check, or overwrite policy; reachability of caller-controlled dest cannot be confirmed from this file alone.

trace.description: The exported helper receives dest from a caller outside this file; no local validation establishes that it is a trusted, fixed path.
The downloaded bytes are synchronously written to the supplied destination without path normalization, containment validation, or a no-overwrite guard.

title: Unbounded synchronous custom JSON parsing permits memory and CPU exhaustion
description: parseJsonCustom synchronously parses a complete caller-provided JSON string and accumulates an entry for every encountered object key in an unbounded array. There is no input-size, nesting, key-count, or execution-time limit in this helper. A request-facing caller can provide a very large JSON document with many object properties, consuming memory for both the original string and result array while monopolizing the Node.js event loop during parser.write().

trace.description: The exported parseJsonCustom function receives jsonString from a caller outside this file, with no size or structural limit applied at this boundary.
Each parsed object key causes a new object to be retained in the result array, making retained memory scale with attacker-controlled key count.

The complete untrusted JSON string is synchronously processed by clarinet via parser.write(), with neither a size bound nor asynchronous yielding; processing and retained results can exhaust process resources.

title: Unauthenticated IDOR permits retrieval of arbitrary baskets
description: The basket-retrieval endpoint is registered without authentication and uses the caller-supplied basket ID as the sole lookup criterion. It neither resolves a current user identity nor scopes the lookup to a basket owner before returning the basket and its products. Consequently, any unauthenticated attacker can enumerate or guess basket IDs and retrieve another customer's basket contents by requesting `/rest/basket/<victim-id>`.

trace.description: The exported handler receives an externally supplied Express request; its caller is outside this file, and architecture context registers it as unauthenticated GET `/rest/basket/:id`.

The handler obtains the target basket identifier directly from the attacker-controlled route parameter and looks up a basket only by `id`. No authentication, owner/user-ID predicate, or other per-basket authorization check exists before use of the result.
The retrieved basket, including its associated products, is serialized into the HTTP response, disclosing the selected basket to the caller.

title: Configuration linter processes unbounded YAML files and file counts
description: The configuration-lint CLI accepts an unbounded number of `.yml` directory entries and reads each entire file into memory before parsing and schema validation. There is no file-count, file-size, parsing-depth, or execution-time limit. If this script is run in CI against contributor-controlled customization files, an attacker can add very large YAML files or many YAML files to exhaust memory/CPU and delay or fail the validation job. Reachability from an untrusted repository/workspace is outside this file, but the absent bounds are visible here.

trace.description: The CLI receives filesystem-controlled configuration directory entries when `main` enumerates the fixed config directory; the caller/workspace that supplies these files is outside this file.
Every entry whose name ends in `.yml` is accepted, sorted, and converted to a path, with no maximum number of files or filtering based on file size/type beyond its suffix.
The loop invokes validation for every accepted file sequentially, so total processing time grows without a configured bound as files are added.

Each file is fully loaded as UTF-8, parsed as YAML, and then subjected to schema validation without a size, depth, or timeout limit; oversized or computationally costly YAML can consume process memory and CPU.

title: Configuration linter follows YAML symlinks outside the configuration directory
description: The linter treats a `.yml` directory entry as a trusted in-directory configuration file but does not reject symbolic links or verify the resolved path remains under `configDir`. `readFile` follows symlinks, so a party able to add an entry in the configuration directory can cause a privileged CI or build invocation to read any file readable by that process. For a target that produces a YAML parse error, the parser error commonly includes source context and is emitted to console logs, potentially disclosing excerpts of the linked file. Whether untrusted users can write this directory or read the resulting logs must be confirmed outside this file.

trace.description: The CLI receives directory entries from the filesystem; the identity and type of each entry are supplied by the workspace outside this file.
A qualifying entry name is joined to `configDir` without `lstat`, realpath containment verification, or a regular-file check. A symlink named `attacker.yml` therefore remains eligible.
The selected path is passed unchanged into `validateFile`.
`readFile` follows the symlink and reads its target; parse failures are caught and the raw parser error is written to console, which can include YAML source context from the target file.

title: Hardcoded JWT RSA private key enables privileged-token forgery
description: The JWT RSA private signing key is embedded in source. Anyone who obtains the source, build artifact, or repository history can use this key to create RS256 JWTs that verify against the corresponding public key. Because privileged middleware makes authorization decisions from signed token role data, a forged token containing an accounting role can pass authorization. The signing key must be externally managed and rotated.

trace.description: The exported authorize function receives a user/claims object from a caller outside this file and creates a JWT from it.
The signing operation uses the RSA private key literal embedded in the source file rather than a protected externally supplied secret.
The fixed key is used to produce RS256 signatures, allowing a party with the exposed key to mint tokens offline.
Accounting authorization accepts a signature-valid token and grants access solely when its signed data.role is accounting; a forged token can therefore reach next().

title: Custom role authorization accepts expired JWTs
description: The custom JWT verification helper calls jws.verify, which verifies only the JWS signature and does not enforce registered JWT claims such as exp. Role checks in isAccounting, isDeluxe, and isCustomer rely on this helper and then trust the decoded claims. Although authorize assigns a six-hour expiration, an otherwise valid token remains accepted after expiration by these custom authorization paths.

trace.description: The exported isAccounting middleware receives an HTTP request from a route registered outside this file.
It obtains the bearer token and invokes the custom verify helper before decoding it.
verify delegates only to jws.verify, with no expiration or other JWT-claim validation.
A token with a valid historical signature and data.role equal to accounting is authorized via next() even if its exp claim has passed.

title: Unauthenticated coupon encoding permits arbitrary discounts
description: Coupon values are merely Z85 encodings of predictable plaintext (MMMyy-discount), not authenticated values. An attacker can encode a current-month payload with any selected numeric discount. The format check is also unanchored and parseInt accepts trailing content, so even the nominal two-digit format does not constrain the parsed value (for example, a payload beginning JUL26-999 is accepted and yields 999). Any checkout or redemption caller trusting discountFromCoupon can be made to apply an arbitrary discount.

trace.description: discountFromCoupon receives a coupon string from its caller outside this file; coupon redemption routes are not visible here.
The caller-controlled value is reversibly decoded with Z85, which provides encoding but neither a signature nor a MAC.
The validation regex is not anchored and only requires a matching substring, allowing a longer discount suffix to pass the check.
The resulting discount component is parsed without a range check and returned for downstream use.

title: Substring-based redirect allowlist can be bypassed
description: The redirect allowlist is enforced with substring matching rather than parsing the URL and comparing its origin to an approved origin. A destination such as https://evil.example/?next=https://github.com/juice-shop/juice-shop or https://github.com/juice-shop/juice-shop@evil.example/ contains an allowlisted string but resolves to an attacker-controlled origin. Any redirect caller using this predicate can be turned into an open redirect; the same weak validation is unsafe if used before server-side URL fetching.

trace.description: isRedirectAllowed receives a destination URL from a caller outside this file, which may be a request-controlled redirect parameter.

Each allowlist entry is tested with url.includes rather than parsing the candidate and comparing scheme, host, and port. An approved URL can therefore be placed in attacker-controlled URL userinfo, path, query, or fragment.

title: Unbounded authenticated-token cache permits memory exhaustion
description: authenticatedUsers retains every token and user object in two process-wide plain-object maps, with no capacity limit, expiration cleanup, or logout removal in this file. Repeated authentication/session creation can monotonically consume heap memory for the process. The maps also retain expired records, making the impact long-lived until restart.

trace.description: The exported put method receives each token and associated user session from callers outside this file.
It inserts the supplied token into a global tokenMap and user ID into a second global idMap without eviction, TTL handling, or a maximum size.

title: Exported security hash helper uses MD5
description: The exported hash helper uses MD5, a collision-broken and fast general-purpose hash. If callers use this helper for passwords, authentication material, signatures, or security-sensitive integrity comparisons, attackers can exploit its lack of password stretching and collision resistance. This file does not show the callers or the data being hashed, so the security-sensitive use is not confirmable here.

trace.description: The exported hash function accepts data from callers outside this file.
It hashes the supplied value using MD5 and returns the digest, providing neither password stretching nor modern collision resistance.

title: Hardcoded HMAC secret permits MAC forgery if helper is used for trust decisions
description: The exported hmac helper has a fixed HMAC secret in source. Any attacker with source or a released artifact can reproduce valid HMACs for arbitrary data. The actual verifier and protected operation are outside this file, so the concrete impact cannot be confirmed here, but embedding a reusable integrity secret defeats the secrecy on which HMAC authentication depends.

trace.description: The exported hmac helper receives data from callers outside this file and computes its integrity tag with a literal source-controlled secret.
The fixed secret is passed directly to createHmac; disclosure of the source lets an attacker compute identical MACs over attacker-chosen data.

title: Unauthenticated order data is interpreted as executable code
description: When either RCE challenge flag is enabled, the unauthenticated order endpoint passes the caller-controlled `orderLinesData` body field to `notevil`'s evaluator. Although the outer VM program is a fixed string, that program explicitly interprets `orderLinesData` as code through `safeEval`. There is no syntax/operation allow-list or data-only parsing before evaluation. An attacker can submit JavaScript/expression payloads in `orderLinesData` and cause the evaluator to interpret them; any evaluator escape or supported dangerous capability becomes server-side code execution. The two-second VM timeout limits an individual synchronous execution but does not make evaluation of attacker-provided code safe.

title: CAPTCHA answer is disclosed and challenge is replayable

description: The publicly reachable coupon endpoint accepts an arbitrary basket ID and updates that basket without authenticating the requester or verifying basket ownership.
