title: Stale authenticated-session state permits overwriting an enrolled MFA secret
description: 2FA setup makes its authorization and state-transition decisions from the user snapshot embedded in an existing authenticated session, rather than from the current database record. A session created before MFA enrollment retains both an empty `totpSecret` and the then-current password hash. An attacker who obtained that session and the password before the victim enrolled in MFA can obtain a server-signed setup secret while the snapshot is empty, then, after the victim enables MFA (or changes their password), submit the previously obtained setup token and old password. The stale checks succeed and the handler overwrites the current database TOTP secret. This permits replacement of the victim's MFA factor and undermines MFA enrollment/password-change remediation. title: Profile image uploads lack visible size and request-rate limits
description: The profile-image endpoint accepts an uploaded file into an in-memory buffer and subsequently writes the entire buffer to disk, but this handler contains no maximum upload-size enforcement or rate limiting. The route is explicitly preceded by memory-storage upload middleware, so requests can force allocation of attacker-controlled file buffers before this handler's file-type check runs. Repeated or very large image uploads can exhaust process memory, disk space in the public uploads directory, and I/O capacity. Any size restriction configured elsewhere in the upload middleware or reverse proxy could mitigate this, but none is visible in this file.

The handler obtains the complete uploaded file buffer from req.file.buffer. File-type detection occurs only after this buffer has already been received and held in memory; no size bound is checked here.

The full attacker-controlled buffer is written to the uploads directory with fs.writeFile, consuming disk and I/O. Repeated uploads can compound the in-memory buffering and disk consumption, with no local throttling or quota control.

title: Unbounded payment-card listing permits excessive resource consumption
description: The payment-method list handler performs an unbounded CardModel.findAll query and builds a complete in-memory response for every card belonging to the resolved user. There is no pagination, limit, cursor, or maximum response size in this handler. An account with a large accumulated card set can repeatedly request GET /api/Cards, forcing unbounded database retrieval, allocation of display objects, card-number masking, and JSON serialization, degrading service availability.

The handler retrieves all Card records for the user with findAll, with no limit, offset, cursor, or pagination constraint.
Every returned record is transformed and the complete array is serialized into the HTTP response, making memory and response work proportional to the unbounded result set.

title: Payment-method deletion and denial events lack handler-level audit logging
description: Deletion of a saved payment method is a security-relevant, potentially fraud-investigation event, but this handler contains no audit/security log for either successful deletion or the rejected deletion attempt. The handler only returns a client response. If card removals are abused, operators cannot reconstruct who attempted the action, what card identifier was targeted, or whether authorization failures are being probed from this code path. Request-wide logging outside this file could mitigate this, but none is visible here.

trace.description: DELETE /api/Cards/:id reaches this exported handler; route registration is outside this file and the handler receives the externally supplied card identifier in req.params.id.
The handler executes the destructive CardModel.destroy operation but has no security/audit logging before or after it; the mutation outcome is only returned to the requester.

title: Windows backslash traversal bypasses quarantine-file restriction
description: The middleware attempts to confine file retrieval to `ftp/quarantine/` by rejecting only forward slashes. That is not a platform-safe path validation control: on Windows, backslash is a path separator, so a route parameter such as `..\..\some-readable-file` contains no `/` and passes the check, but is interpreted by `path.resolve` as traversal outside the quarantine directory. Because `sendFile` receives the resulting absolute path without a `root` restriction or a post-resolution containment check, an attacker can retrieve files readable by the service account outside the intended directory.

The caller-controlled route parameter is copied into `file`.
The only validation rejects `/`; it does not reject Windows backslash separators or verify that the resolved path remains under the quarantine directory.
`path.resolve` interprets attacker-supplied backslashes as separators on Windows and the resulting absolute path is supplied to `sendFile`, permitting reads outside `ftp/quarantine/`.

title: Wallet mint verification lacks proof of wallet ownership
description: The wallet verification endpoint treats a caller-supplied wallet address as proof that the caller owns that wallet. Any party can observe an NFTMinted event and its minter address on the public blockchain, then submit that address to this unauthenticated endpoint before the actual minter does. The server will consume the address from its pending set and return a successful challenge completion without requiring a wallet signature, a connected authenticated identity, or any other proof of control. This allows theft/consumption of another user's mint-verification result and falsely attributes successful completion to an arbitrary caller.

trace.description: The exported POST /rest/web3/walletNFTVerify handler receives attacker-controlled input from an external caller; route registration is outside this file and applies no authentication middleware according to the supplied route context.
The handler obtains walletAddress directly from the request body, without associating it with an authenticated principal or validating a wallet-signed challenge.

The authorization decision is solely membership of the caller-asserted address in a global set populated from public NFTMinted events. No signature verification or per-user ownership check occurs before the result is consumed.
A matching attacker-supplied address is deleted and produces a successful challenge result, permanently preventing the rightful minter from using that pending event in this process.

title: Concurrent listener requests can create unbounded persistent WebSocket subscriptions
description: The unauthenticated listener-creation endpoint has a check-then-await race. Concurrent requests can all observe isEventListenerCreated as false, suspend at the dynamic import, and subsequently each create a separate persistent WebSocketProvider and NFTMinted subscription before any invocation sets the flag at line 29. These subscriptions are never closed on normal operation. An attacker can issue concurrent GET requests to create multiple long-lived outbound WebSocket connections and event handlers, consuming application connections, memory, and provider quota; error handling also resets the flag, enabling later recreation attempts.

trace.description: The exported GET /rest/web3/nftMintListen handler is externally reachable without authentication according to the supplied route context.
Each request tests the global listener flag but does not atomically reserve listener creation before asynchronous work begins.
The dynamic import introduces an await point after the flag check, allowing simultaneous requests that already passed the check to continue independently.
Every racing invocation creates a new outbound WebSocketProvider connection to Alchemy; no request throttling, connection cap, or cleanup is present in this handler.
Each created provider is registered with a persistent NFTMinted event subscription, retaining the associated connection and callback beyond the HTTP request.

title: Unrestricted user-controlled URL fetch enables SSRF and internal response exposure
description: The authenticated profile-image URL workflow sends a server-side request to the caller-supplied `imageUrl` without parsing it or enforcing an origin, scheme, hostname, resolved-IP, or private-network allow-list. The only URL-related check is a challenge marker and does not restrict the destination. An authenticated attacker can submit URLs such as `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/`, cloud metadata endpoints, or internal service addresses. The fetched response is then written into a publicly reachable profile-image location, potentially allowing the attacker to exfiltrate response contents by loading their resulting profile image, as well as interact with internal HTTP services. Redirects are also handled by `fetch` without an application-level destination check.

trace.description: The exported handler receives an Express request from the route caller outside this file; `req.body.imageUrl` is attacker-controlled request-body input.
The handler copies the caller-provided image URL into `url`. The subsequent regex only sets a challenge flag for one string pattern and is not a destination validation or allow-list.
`fetch(url)` makes an outbound request to the fully attacker-controlled destination without validation, enabling requests to loopback, private-network, metadata, or other internal HTTP endpoints.

title: Unbounded remote image download permits disk and connection exhaustion
description: The endpoint streams the complete body of an attacker-selected remote response to disk without checking `Content-Length`, enforcing a byte limit, applying a download timeout, or aborting a slow/infinite response. An authenticated attacker can point `imageUrl` at an arbitrarily large file or an endpoint that continuously streams bytes, repeatedly invoke the route, and consume disk capacity and keep server-side connections/streaming work occupied. The extension check does not constrain response size or content.

trace.description: The exported handler receives the external HTTP request from a caller outside this file, including the attacker-controlled `req.body.imageUrl` field.
The untrusted image URL is assigned to `url`; no request-body URL constraint establishes a maximum remote resource size or download duration.
The handler obtains a response body from the attacker-selected remote URL. No content-length limit, timeout, or abort signal is supplied to bound the download.
The entire remote response body is piped into a file and awaited to completion with no byte/count limit. A very large or never-ending body can exhaust disk and tie up streams/connections.

title: Unauthenticated notification replay endpoint permits unlimited event triggering
description: The publicly reachable GET endpoint accepts an arbitrary challenge name and, when that globally tracked challenge is solved, re-emits its notification. There is no authentication, authorization, ownership, or server-side event-origin check tying the request to the user/session that solved the challenge. An unauthenticated attacker can repeatedly call `/rest/repeat-notification?challenge=<solved-challenge-name>` to replay challenge notifications, potentially misleading connected users and generating an unbounded stream of notification work. The route has no declared authentication middleware, and the handler contains no throttling or replay protection.

trace.description: The exported handler receives attacker-controlled query data from the GET route; its caller and route registration are outside this file, and the supplied route context states that no authentication middleware protects it.
The caller-controlled `query.challenge` value is decoded and used to resolve a challenge by name, allowing the requester to select which challenge's state is inspected.

If the selected challenge is globally marked solved, the handler triggers `sendNotification(challenge, true)` with no caller identity, authorization, replay protection, or rate limit. Repeated unauthenticated requests can therefore cause repeated notification dispatches.

title: Unthrottled public redirect endpoint
description: The public redirect endpoint contains no application-level rate limiting or other throttling before generating a response. An attacker can repeatedly request `/redirect?to=<allowlisted-url>` to force unlimited redirect responses and associated error handling/network work. Each request is low-cost, so this is low severity, and reverse-proxy or infrastructure controls may mitigate it but are not visible in this file.

trace.description: The exported handler receives externally supplied query data; its route caller is outside this file and is registered as unauthenticated GET /redirect.
The caller-controlled `to` query parameter is read into `toUrl`; no request-rate or per-client consumption control is applied on this path.
For every request passing the allowlist predicate, the handler immediately creates a redirect response without a visible throttle, allowing repeated requests to consume service capacity.

title: SQL injection in unauthenticated product search
description: The public product-search handler interpolates the caller-controlled `q` value directly into two SQL `LIKE` literals in a raw query. The only preceding control truncates the value to 200 characters; it does not escape quotes or bind the value as a query parameter. An attacker can supply a quote plus SQL syntax (for example, a boolean predicate and SQL comment appropriate to the database) to alter the WHERE clause, extract data through UNION/error-based techniques, or bypass the intended `deletedAt IS NULL` product filter.

trace.description: The exported search handler receives externally supplied request data; its caller/route registration is outside this file, and the documented GET /rest/products/search route is unauthenticated.
The handler reads the attacker-controlled `q` query parameter and only applies a length cap. Quotes and SQL metacharacters remain intact.

`criteria` is interpolated into a raw SQL template literal twice and passed to `sequelize.query` without bound parameters or an allow-list, causing the database to interpret attacker input as SQL structure.

title: Unbounded unauthenticated product-search results
description: The unauthenticated search endpoint executes an ordered `SELECT *` and serializes every matching product without a LIMIT, offset, cursor, or page-size cap. Repeated requests, including broad searches such as an empty `q`, can force full matching result sets to be read, sorted, translated in a per-product loop, and placed in a JSON response. The route and handler show no throttling. This can consume database CPU, application memory, and response bandwidth; infrastructure limits outside this file may mitigate but are not visible here.

trace.description: The exported handler receives requests to the documented unauthenticated GET /rest/products/search route; route registration is outside this file.
An omitted `q` is converted to an empty search criterion, permitting a broad search; the only limit is on criterion length, not result count or request frequency.

The raw query has no pagination or result limit and orders all matches. All returned rows are then processed and serialized, creating an attacker-triggerable database/CPU/memory/bandwidth consumption sink.

title: Forgeable continuation codes authorize arbitrary challenge completion
description: The unauthenticated continuation-code endpoint treats a Hashids value as authorization to mark arbitrary challenges solved, but its fixed salt is embedded in source. Hashids is a reversible obfuscation scheme rather than a signed/authenticated token format; anyone with the source (or the deployed artifact) can instantiate Hashids with this salt and encode chosen challenge IDs. An attacker can therefore forge a syntactically valid continuation code containing every known challenge ID and cause their progress to be restored/marked solved without possessing a legitimately issued code. The same defect is repeated by the Find-It and Fix-It variants with separate hardcoded salts.

trace.description: The exported handler receives the externally supplied `:continueCode` route parameter; its caller/route registration is outside this file, and architecture context shows this endpoint has no authentication middleware.

The handler constructs Hashids with the hardcoded source-visible salt `this is my salt`; this supplies no secret, cryptographic integrity check, expiry, or binding to a user/session for the continuation capability.

The attacker-controlled route parameter is accepted after only an alphanumeric format check and decoded into attacker-selected numeric IDs. The check does not establish that the code was issued by the application.

Every decoded ID matching a challenge causes `challengeUtils.solve(challenge, true)` to mark that challenge solved. Thus a forged code directly changes completion state. Equivalent decode-and-solve paths exist at lines 44-49 and 65-70 using likewise hardcoded salts at lines 39 and 59.

title: JSON path parameter can inject ORM predicate operators into recycle lookup
description: The public item lookup parses the path segment as arbitrary JSON and places the resulting value directly in the ORM's `where.id` predicate. This permits a caller to provide an object or array rather than the intended scalar identifier. In Sequelize configurations accepting legacy/string operator aliases, a URL-encoded value such as `{"$ne":-1}` can turn the equality lookup into an operator predicate and cause `findAll` to return records other than the requested item. No scalar-type validation or operator allow-list occurs before the query. This both exposes the query structure to caller control and removes the expected one-item bound on the response; exploitation depends on the application's Sequelize operator-alias configuration.

trace.description: The exported handler receives the externally routed request; the route registration is outside this file, and the supplied `:id` path parameter is available as `req.params.id`.

`req.params.id` is parsed as unrestricted JSON, so an attacker can submit an object/array instead of a scalar recycle identifier; the parsed result is assigned directly to the `id` condition without type validation or an operator allow-list.

`findAll` executes the caller-influenced `where.id` structure. Accepted ORM operator objects can broaden the predicate, while `findAll` has no limit or pagination and serializes every matched record into the response.

title: Unsanitized client IP header persisted as stored-XSS payload
description: When the HTTP-header XSS challenge is enabled, the handler deliberately skips sanitization of the caller-controlled `true-client-ip` header and persists it as `lastLoginIp`. Converting the value to a string does not provide HTML/contextual encoding. An authenticated attacker can send a header such as ``; if this login-IP field is subsequently displayed in an administrative/account view without correct output encoding, it becomes stored XSS. The persistence point is the appropriate reporting location because the eventual rendering sink is outside this file.

trace.description: The exported handler receives the HTTP request from a caller/route registration outside this file.
It reads `true-client-ip` directly from request headers, which an HTTP client can supply or spoof unless a trusted proxy has stripped and set this header.
When the HTTP-header XSS challenge is enabled, the branch at this condition leaves the header unsanitized; only the alternative branch calls `sanitizeSecure`.
The unencoded header value is written to the user's `lastLoginIp` datastore field. Any later UI rendering of that stored value is outside this file.

title: Caller-controlled header can forge login-IP audit data
description: The endpoint treats a request-provided `true-client-ip` header as the authoritative login source address. It uses the actual socket remote address only when the header is absent, and does not establish that the header was inserted by a trusted reverse proxy or that its value is a valid IP address. Thus, any authenticated user can repeatedly replace the recorded login source with an arbitrary value, corrupting security/audit evidence and frustrating login-location monitoring and incident investigation.

The handler selects `true-client-ip` from attacker-controlled request headers before considering the socket address.
The real peer address is used only if the header is undefined, so supplying any header bypasses use of the server-observed source address.
The selected, unverified value is persisted as `lastLoginIp`, making the manipulated value the recorded login-IP evidence.

title: Unthrottled login-IP update endpoint permits database write amplification
description: Each authenticated request performs a primary-key lookup followed by a database update, but this handler contains no rate limit, debounce, or other request-frequency control. A token holder can automate requests to this GET endpoint and force sustained database reads/writes, potentially consuming connection and write capacity. Rate limiting may exist at infrastructure scope, which cannot be verified from this file.

For every authenticated request, it performs a database primary-key lookup for the user.
It then issues a database update on every request, with no rate-limiting or coalescing control present in this handler.

title: Unauthenticated IDOR permits checkout of arbitrary baskets
description: The unauthenticated checkout route looks up a basket solely by the caller-supplied path ID. Although it obtains an optional authenticated user later, it never requires authentication and never compares a basket owner/UserId to that user. Any caller can submit another customer's basket ID, causing that basket's items to be removed and receiving an order confirmation for it.

BasketModel.findOne uses only the supplied ID. The later identity lookup is optional and there is no ownership or authorization comparison before the checkout continues.
Checkout destroys every BasketItem associated with the caller-selected basket, completing the unauthorized mutation; the response subsequently confirms the order.

title: Caller-controlled UserId selects the wallet charged for an order
description: The handler treats req.body.UserId as the authority for which wallet pays and receives points. It does not derive the wallet account from the authenticated customer, and the route is reachable with no authentication middleware. An attacker can provide a victim's UserId together with paymentId "wallet" to debit that victim's wallet for an attacker-selected basket, provided the victim has sufficient balance. The attacker can likewise direct earned points to arbitrary accounts.

trace.description: The exported request handler accepts externally supplied request-body fields; the route registration is outside this file and the provided route context shows no authentication middleware.
The payment and rewards logic accepts UserId directly from req.body rather than deriving it from security.authenticatedUsers.from(req).
The supplied UserId is used as the wallet lookup criterion, with no comparison to the optional customer identity collected at lines 38-39.
The selected wallet is debited for totalPrice when the caller supplies paymentId "wallet", making the arbitrary-account selection financially consequential.

title: Checkout permits orders without any successful payment
description: Payment is optional by design in this handler. The only wallet-debit block is guarded by req.body.UserId; omitting that field skips all payment enforcement, yet the handler has already decremented inventory and still persists an order with a caller-controlled (or null) paymentId. Thus a caller can check out a basket without payment by omitting UserId, potentially obtaining an order eligible for fulfillment while avoiding any charge.

trace.description: The exported checkout handler receives the attacker-controlled request body from the external route caller.
The handler decrements product inventory while processing the basket, before any payment condition is enforced.
All wallet payment handling is conditional on req.body.UserId, so a request that omits UserId takes no payment path.
Regardless of whether a payment occurred, the handler inserts an order record, including a null or caller-supplied paymentId, and later completes the order document/confirmation flow.

title: Concurrent checkout requests can oversell and corrupt inventory
description: Stock accounting is a non-atomic read-modify-write with neither an availability check nor a transaction/idempotency guard. Parallel requests for the same basket can both read the same quantity before basket deletion occurs and each subtract the ordered amount. This permits negative inventory and duplicate checkout processing/orders, corrupting stock and potentially overselling products.

trace.description: The checkout handler is an externally invocable request entrypoint and accepts repeated requests for the same basket ID.
For each basket item, it reads the current inventory quantity without locking or transaction scope.
It calculates the replacement value by subtracting the basket quantity, without checking that sufficient stock remains and without marking the basket as already checked out.

The independently computed quantity is written back via a separate update. Two simultaneous requests can each perform this update and drive inventory below zero or account for the same purchase multiple times.

title: Forgeable client coupon data grants campaign discounts
description: couponData is accepted as a base64-encoded client assertion and interpreted as a coupon code plus campaign date. Base64 provides no authenticity: an attacker can construct, for example, the encoding of a hardcoded campaign code and its validOn timestamp. The check compares those attacker-reproducible values to public constants rather than verifying a server-issued, signed, or redeemed coupon, then applies up to a 75% discount. It also does not verify that the campaign is currently valid.

trace.description: The checkout handler accepts the externally supplied request body containing couponData.
couponData is base64-decoded and split into code and date fields. Base64 is reversible encoding rather than an integrity/authenticity control.
The caller-controlled fields are compared only to hardcoded campaign values; no signature, issuance record, redemption state, or current-date check is used.
The returned campaign discount is used to calculate the amount deducted from the purchase price.

title: Unauthenticated checkout can be abused to exhaust PDF generation and disk resources
description: Each unauthenticated checkout request dynamically loads PDFKit, creates a PDF document, and writes a uniquely named file under ftp/. No rate limit, quota, request-level idempotency control, or cleanup is present in this handler. An attacker can issue many requests (including against a valid basket before its asynchronous cleanup completes) to consume CPU, database capacity, and especially disk space through persistent PDFs. Deployment-level throttling may mitigate this but is not visible here.

trace.description: The exported checkout handler is the external request entrypoint; the provided routing context shows POST /rest/basket/:id has no authentication or authorization middleware.
Every successful basket lookup imports and instantiates PDFKit as part of request processing.
The handler writes a unique order PDF to the ftp directory, with no visible rate, storage, or per-request resource limit before this persistent filesystem operation.

title: Password-reset security answers can be brute-forced without rate limiting
description: The unauthenticated password-recovery endpoint performs a security-answer authentication decision and password-reset operation without any visible per-IP, per-account, or per-endpoint attempt limit. An attacker can repeatedly submit guesses for a known victim email until a security-question answer is found. Each attempt also causes a database join/query, and a successful guess changes the victim's credential. This is both unrestricted resource consumption and an authentication failure because rate-limit-free recovery attempts permit online brute force of the recovery factor.

trace.description: The exported handler receives unauthenticated attacker-controlled reset fields from the POST route; the caller and route registration are outside this file.
The handler accepts caller-controlled email and security-answer values. No attempt counter, delay, lockout, or throttling check occurs before these values are used in recovery verification.
Every submitted guess reaches a database lookup joining the supplied email to a security-answer record, consuming database resources for unlimited unauthenticated requests.
The supplied answer's HMAC is compared to the stored recovery answer and a match authorizes the password-reset path; no rate limit or lockout protects this authentication decision.

title: Reset flow accepts arbitrary weak passwords
description: The handler's only password-quality controls are that `new` be nonempty and equal `repeat`; it accepts arbitrary weak values such as a single-character password. On a valid security-answer recovery request, that value is persisted as the account password. This weak credential policy materially reduces the effort to compromise an account once an attacker can invoke or complete recovery; password-strength validation may exist in model code outside this file, so that cannot be confirmed here.

Caller-controlled `body.new` is assigned to `newPassword`.

The visible validation rejects only empty or literal `undefined` values and checks equality with the repeated value; it imposes no length, complexity, breached-password, or other strength requirement.
After recovery authentication succeeds, the unvalidated password is persisted through `user.update`.

title: Successful password resets are not security logged
description: A successful password reset is a security-relevant account-recovery and credential-change event, but this handler emits no audit log or security event when it updates the password. The response is returned directly after the update. This prevents reliable detection and investigation of unauthorized recovery attempts that succeed; centralized logging outside this file cannot be verified from the shown code.

Following successful recovery-answer verification, the handler locates the account whose credential will be changed.
The password is updated and the handler proceeds to return the user response without a visible audit/logging call recording the reset, account, source address, or outcome.

title: NoSQL JavaScript injection through product review ID
description: The product identifier is concatenated into a MongoDB `$where` JavaScript expression rather than supplied as a typed/parameterized query value. When `noSqlCommandChallenge` is enabled, the handler uses a merely length-truncated string instead of numeric coercion, allowing a caller to terminate or alter the comparison expression. For example, an `id` such as `1 || true` causes the `$where` predicate to match reviews for every product, while JavaScript statements/functions can be injected into the database-side expression. The 40-character truncation is not an allow-list or a safe query construction mechanism.

`req.params.id` is converted to a string truncated only to 40 characters whenever the NoSQL-command challenge is enabled. This preserves JavaScript operators and statement syntax.

The tainted `id` is concatenated into the `$where` JavaScript source passed to the review collection. No parameter binding or syntactic allow-list intervenes, so MongoDB interprets attacker input as query code.

title: Injected $where expressions enable repeated query-delay denial of service
description: The same injectable `$where` execution can be used to consume server/database CPU. The file explicitly provides a blocking `sleep` primitive, capped at 2 seconds, and the `$where` code path is reachable without authentication or visible per-client rate limiting. An attacker can inject a short expression such as `1; sleep(2000)` (subject to the MongoDB execution environment) and issue many concurrent requests, tying up query workers and degrading review availability. The two-second cap limits an individual delay but does not prevent aggregate exhaustion.

trace.description: The exported review handler receives externally supplied route parameters; route registration is outside this file, and architecture context shows this GET route has no authentication middleware.
When the challenge is enabled, the user-supplied ID remains a JavaScript-capable string after only a 40-character truncation.
This file defines a synchronous `sleep` function and only caps a single invocation at 2,000 ms; it does not impose a request/concurrency limit.

The interpolated value is executed as part of MongoDB's `$where` JavaScript predicate. Injected delay code can make each request expensive, and repeated concurrent requests can exhaust available processing capacity.

title: Account enumeration through unauthenticated security-question recovery lookup
description: The unauthenticated security-question lookup reveals whether an arbitrary email address belongs to an account: existing accounts produce a response containing a security question, whereas nonexistent accounts receive an empty object. Because this endpoint is part of the security-question/account-recovery flow, the distinguishable response permits account enumeration and lets an attacker target known accounts with recovery-answer guessing or social engineering.

The handler takes the attacker-supplied email query parameter as the account identifier.
The supplied email is used to look up a User-associated SecurityAnswer, making the response dependent on whether that email maps to an account with a security answer.

When no matching answer/account exists, the handler emits {}, while the alternate branch at line 23 emits a question object. This observable difference discloses account existence and recovery-question availability without authentication.

title: Unauthenticated recovery lookup has no visible rate limit
description: The public endpoint performs a joined user/security-answer lookup and, for every match, an additional security-question lookup, but this handler contains no throttling or request-cost control. An attacker can repeatedly submit arbitrary email values to force database work, causing avoidable database load and amplifying account-enumeration attempts. A global rate limit may exist outside this file, so that mitigation cannot be assessed here.

An attacker controls the email value used as the lookup key and can submit unlimited distinct or repeated values.
Each request causes a SecurityAnswer/User join lookup; no local rate limit, quota, or cache is applied before this database operation.

title: Unbounded global timestamp accumulation on public feedback route
description: The unauthenticated POST /api/Feedbacks middleware records one timestamp per request in a process-global application-local array and monotonically increments its index. It neither expires nor bounds retained entries. An attacker can repeatedly POST to this endpoint to grow captchaBypassReqTimes for the lifetime of the process, consuming heap memory and eventually degrading or crashing the service.

Each request writes a newly allocated timestamp to req.app.locals.captchaBypassReqTimes at a globally increasing index and increments captchaReqId. No size cap, expiration, cleanup, or request throttling is present in this handler, making the global array the unbounded memory-consumption sink.

title: Authenticated users can modify reviews owned by other users
description: The handler obtains the authenticated user but never uses that identity to scope the review selection or verify review ownership. Any authenticated account can submit another review's identifier and replace its message. The route's authentication middleware only establishes that the caller is logged in; it does not authorize the caller to modify the selected review.

The handler resolves the authenticated user, but the resulting user value is not used in a review-owner or authorization comparison.
The update selects a review solely by caller-controlled req.body.id and writes caller-controlled content. There is no author/user predicate in the selector before the mutation executes.

title: NoSQL operator injection permits bulk review modification
description: The request body's id value is inserted directly into a MongoDB query selector. Because it is not constrained to a scalar identifier, an attacker can provide a MongoDB operator object such as {"$ne": null} in place of id. With multi:true, the update can then match and overwrite every review's message rather than a single intended review. This is NoSQL operator injection with a direct data-integrity impact.

trace.description: The exported handler accepts an Express request whose body is attacker-controlled; the route caller is outside this file.
The unvalidated req.body.id value is placed directly into the MongoDB selector as _id, allowing an object supplied by the caller to occupy a query-operator position.
The collection update executes the attacker-influenced selector with multi:true, so an injected selector such as {_id: {$ne: null}} can update all matching reviews.

title: Unsanitized review message can introduce stored cross-site scripting
description: The endpoint persists arbitrary caller-controlled review message text without sanitization or a content allow-list. Review messages are a display-oriented field and may be rendered later in a browser; a payload such as an event-handler-bearing HTML element becomes stored XSS if the downstream review renderer does not apply context-appropriate output encoding. The rendering sink is outside this file, but the unsafe persistence point is visible here.

The message field is read directly from the request body without sanitization, encoding, or an allow-list appropriate for browser-rendered review content.
The MongoDB $set operation persists the untrusted message as the review text, creating the stored-XSS persistence point.

title: Unauthenticated `$where` JavaScript injection exposes all orders and can exhaust MongoDB
description: When the reflected-XSS challenge is enabled, the order ID is only truncated and is then interpolated directly into a MongoDB `$where` JavaScript expression. Truncation neither escapes single quotes nor restricts JavaScript syntax. An unauthenticated caller can supply an ID such as `' || true || '` to turn the predicate into `this.orderId === '' || true || ''`, causing the query to match every order. The resulting order documents are returned directly. Because `$where` executes server-side JavaScript and no execution limit is set here, crafted input can also invoke computationally expensive or non-terminating JavaScript and tie up MongoDB query processing.

trace.description: The exported route handler receives an externally supplied `:id` path parameter through `req.params.id`; its caller/route registration is outside this file, and the provided route context shows it is reachable without authentication.

When `reflectedXssChallenge` is enabled, the attacker-controlled ID passes only through `utils.trunc(..., 60)`. This preserves quotes and JavaScript operators, so it is not an escaping or allow-listing control for a JavaScript `$where` expression.

The unescaped ID is template-interpolated inside the `$where` JavaScript source and executed by MongoDB. A payload such as `' || true || '` bypasses the equality condition and matches all documents; server-side JavaScript payloads can also consume excessive query CPU.
The matched query results are serialized into the HTTP response without authentication or a per-order ownership check, disclosing every order selected by the injected predicate.

title: Client-controlled wallet top-up amount creates arbitrary credit
description: The wallet top-up workflow trusts a client-supplied balance delta after only checking that the supplied payment card exists and belongs to the request user. It neither charges the card nor derives, bounds, or records an amount server-side. An authenticated user with any valid saved card can submit an arbitrary positive value (and repeat the request) to mint wallet credit; negative values may also reduce a balance unexpectedly. This is an economic-integrity design failure rather than a property-binding issue because the sensitive balance mutation is explicitly performed using an untrusted value.

trace.description: The exported PUT handler receives an attacker-controlled HTTP request; route registration/caller is outside this file. The route's appendUserId middleware may establish UserId, but it does not establish the monetary amount.
The handler reads the caller-provided payment identifier from the request body.

The only payment-related validation is a lookup that confirms the card ID belongs to UserId. There is no charge, authorization, transaction state, amount derivation, amount limit, or one-time-use control.

The persistent wallet balance is incremented by req.body.balance, a value directly controlled by the caller. Supplying a large positive amount after selecting a valid owned card credits that amount without corresponding payment.

title: Wallet balance changes lack security audit logging
description: Wallet-credit mutations are security-relevant financial events, but this handler emits no audit log for successful top-ups, the identity/card used, the requested amount, or failures. Consequently, repeated arbitrary-credit requests and fraudulent balance changes cannot be reliably detected or investigated from application security logs.

trace.description: The exported PUT handler receives external requests that initiate wallet-balance changes; the route caller is outside this file.
After a card lookup succeeds, the handler enters the successful financial-mutation path without recording an audit event.
The handler updates the wallet balance and returns success, but performs no logging of the account, payment identifier, amount, result, or correlation information.

title: Unbounded attacker-controlled code-fix cache permits memory and event-loop exhaustion
description: Both publicly reachable handlers accept an attacker-controlled challenge key and pass it to a process-global cache without a length, character-set, or cardinality limit. Every previously unseen key causes synchronous directory enumeration and then inserts a new entry, including entries with no matching fixes. An attacker can issue requests containing many distinct keys to grow `CodeFixes` without bound; the synchronous filesystem work also blocks Node.js's event loop for each cache miss. This can consume heap/CPU and degrade or deny service.

trace.description: The externally reachable GET handler receives the caller-controlled `:key` path parameter; route registration is outside this file and the supplied architecture context identifies this handler as unauthenticated.
The unvalidated key is passed directly into `readFixes`, where a cache miss triggers synchronous directory enumeration; arbitrary distinct keys all miss unless previously cached.
After scanning, `readFixes` permanently stores an entry under the caller-controlled key, even when `fixes` is empty. There is no eviction or maximum cache size.

title: Unauthenticated verdict endpoint processes unbounded selected-lines arrays
description: The unauthenticated POST /snippets/verdict handler accepts an unbounded caller-controlled selectedLines array and performs per-element processing without any local request-size, array-length, or rate-limit control. An attacker can repeatedly submit very large arrays, causing linear memory/CPU work in filter/includes processing; each request also reaches challenge lookup and filesystem/YAML operations. This can degrade service availability, particularly because the route has no authentication middleware.

trace.description: The exported checkVulnLines handler receives externally supplied POST request data in req.body; the registered /snippets/verdict route has no authentication middleware, and no size, count, or rate control is implemented in this handler.
The handler assigns the caller-controlled req.body.selectedLines value to selectedLines without runtime validation or a maximum length, then passes it to getVerdict.

getVerdict filters every submitted element and invokes includes against the allowed-line array for each element. A very large selectedLines array therefore causes attacker-controlled CPU and memory work; no preceding bound or throttling limits this operation.

title: Stored username is evaluated as server-side JavaScript
description: The handler evaluates JavaScript extracted from the authenticated user's stored username. A username matching `#{...}` reaches `eval()` whenever the username-XSS challenge is enabled. If an attacker can set their username through the application's registration/profile functionality, arbitrary server-side JavaScript executes in the Node.js process under the application's privileges; for example, a username containing `#{process.mainModule.require('node:child_process').execSync('id')}`. The guard is only a pattern match and challenge flag, not a restriction on executable content.

trace.description: The exported profile handler receives an Express request; its route registration is outside this file (and architecture context shows GET /profile has no route middleware).
The handler resolves the request cookie to an authenticated-user record, selecting the profile associated with the supplied session token.
It loads the selected user's database record by the server-derived user ID.
The stored username is copied into the value later processed as template/code content. The endpoint which initially persists a username is outside this file.
A username syntactically shaped as `#{...}` has its interior extracted when the challenge feature is enabled; no allow-list or other validation of the extracted program is performed.
The extracted username content is interpreted by JavaScript `eval`, allowing attacker-controlled stored username content to execute on the server.

title: Unauthenticated profile requests trigger repeated filesystem work before authentication
description: GET /profile performs a filesystem read before it verifies that the requester has an authenticated token, and there is no throttling or request-cost control in this handler. An unauthenticated attacker can repeatedly request this route and force the application to initiate repeated reads of `views/userProfile.pug`; authenticated attackers can additionally cause Pug template compilation on every request. The route is declared without middleware in the supplied routing context, so this expensive pre-authentication work is directly reachable from the network. Upstream rate limiting could mitigate this, but it is not visible in this file.

trace.description: The exported handler receives each GET /profile request; its caller/route registration is outside this file, and the supplied route context specifies no authentication middleware.
The handler enters its processing path and attempts to load the profile template before resolving or validating the caller's session token.
Each request awaits a filesystem read of the Pug template; this resource-consuming operation is reachable before the authentication rejection at lines 34-37 and has no visible rate limit.

title: Unsanitized profile username can introduce stored XSS
description: The profile endpoint persists the caller-controlled username without validation, sanitization, or output encoding. If this profile value is subsequently rendered in an HTML-capable profile, account, or administrative view without context-appropriate encoding, an attacker can save markup such as an event-handler payload and cause stored XSS when that profile is viewed. The rendering sink is outside this file, but the unsafe persistence point is present here.

trace.description: The exported profile-update handler receives externally supplied request data; its route caller is outside this file.
The handler reads the attacker-controlled body property req.body.username directly while handling the authenticated user's profile update.
The username is persisted through the ORM update with no visible character allow-list, sanitization, or encoding. A later HTML rendering sink outside this file could interpret stored markup/script.

title: Authentication token cookie lacks security attributes
description: The replacement authentication token is set with Express's default cookie options. No HttpOnly, Secure, or SameSite attributes are supplied. In particular, absence of HttpOnly makes the bearer token readable by any JavaScript executing in the application's origin (including a successful XSS payload), enabling session theft and replay. Absence of Secure also permits transmission over a non-HTTPS connection if one is reachable.

trace.description: The exported handler is reached from external HTTP input and operates on the caller's authenticated session; route registration is outside this file.
After updating the account, the handler creates a new token representing the user's authenticated identity.
The bearer token is issued as a cookie with res.cookie('token', updatedToken) and no options. Express therefore does not set HttpOnly, Secure, or SameSite for this cookie.

title: Repeated profile updates may grow the authentication-token store indefinitely
description: Every successful profile request creates and stores a newly authorized token, but this handler never removes the token supplied in req.cookies.token. An authenticated attacker can repeatedly change their username and cause session entries to accumulate, consuming the authenticated-user token store and potentially memory. The capacity and TTL behavior of authenticatedUsers are outside this file, so an external bounded/expiring cache could mitigate the impact, but neither a cleanup operation nor request throttling is visible on this path.

trace.description: The exported handler accepts repeated external POST requests; the caller and route middleware are outside this file.
Each request that has a valid session token is accepted and produces a newly authorized token after the profile update.
The new token is added to authenticatedUsers, while no removal or invalidation of the previous req.cookies.token appears on this path. Repeated requests can therefore add stale session records.

title: Unauthenticated video range requests can create unlimited file streams
description: The unauthenticated GET /video handler has no visible request-rate, connection, or concurrent-stream limit. A caller can repeatedly send valid Range requests, causing each request to open a new filesystem read stream and retain a response connection while video bytes are transmitted. Requests for small overlapping ranges can amplify file-descriptor, socket, disk-I/O, and bandwidth consumption without requiring a large request body. Infrastructure throttling could mitigate this, but no such control is present in this handler.

trace.description: The exported getVideo handler receives an externally initiated request; its caller/route registration is outside this file, and architecture context maps it to unauthenticated GET /video.
The handler accepts the caller-controlled Range header and enters the partial-content path whenever it is present, with no per-client rate, concurrency, or request-cost control.
Each accepted request creates a new read stream for the video and pipes it to the client, consuming a file descriptor, disk I/O, outbound bandwidth, and a response connection until completion.

title: Unauthenticated promotion endpoint recompiles template on every request without throttling
description: The unauthenticated GET /promotion endpoint performs filesystem reads, synchronously reads subtitle data, and compiles a Pug template separately for every request. There is no visible throttling or caching of the compiled output. An attacker can issue concurrent requests to repeatedly force CPU work and filesystem activity, degrading service availability. The fixed template/subtitle sizes limit per-request cost, so this is lower impact than an unbounded input-based CPU attack, but repeated unauthenticated work remains exploitable for resource exhaustion.

trace.description: The exported promotionVideo handler receives an externally initiated request; its caller/route registration is outside this file, and architecture context maps it to unauthenticated GET /promotion.
For every request, the handler reads the promotion template and obtains subtitle content rather than serving a cached result.
getSubsFromFile synchronously reads the subtitle asset during request processing, adding blocking filesystem work to each request.
The handler compiles the Pug template on every request; without a visible rate/concurrency limit or compiled-template cache, concurrent requests can repeatedly consume CPU.

title: Concurrent requests bypass the listener initialization guard and create unbounded WebSocket connections
description: The one-time listener guard is not concurrency-safe. `isEventListenerCreated` is tested before an `await`, but is only set after the WebSocket provider and contract listener have already been constructed. Concurrent unauthenticated POST requests can all observe `false`, suspend at the dynamic import, and subsequently each create an Alchemy WebSocket connection and event listener. An attacker can issue parallel requests to exhaust application sockets, provider connection quotas, memory, or event-processing capacity.

trace.description: The exported handler receives an attacker-controlled HTTP request; its caller/route registration is outside this file, and architecture context identifies it as unauthenticated POST /rest/web3/walletExploitAddress.
Each request checks the shared initialization flag, but no lock or promise is installed before asynchronous work begins.
The dynamic import yields execution while the flag remains false; parallel handlers can therefore pass the same guard before any handler reaches the assignment at line 31.
Every racing handler creates a new WebSocketProvider connection using the Alchemy endpoint before initialization is marked complete, consuming outbound connections and associated resources.

title: Unauthenticated wallet registration grows a global Set without bounds
description: Every unauthenticated request inserts the caller-provided `walletAddress` into a process-global Set. There is no validation, rate limit, maximum Set size, expiration, or cleanup for addresses that never appear in a ContractExploited event. An attacker can send many requests with unique address strings (or distinct JSON values accepted by the body parser), causing the Set to grow for the process lifetime and eventually exhaust memory.

trace.description: The exported handler receives a request from outside this file; architecture context identifies the route as unauthenticated POST /rest/web3/walletExploitAddress.
The handler takes walletAddress directly from the attacker-controlled request body, with no format validation or request-rate/quantity control visible in this handler.
The supplied value is retained in the process-global walletsConnected Set. Entries are only removed when a matching external contract event occurs, so arbitrary unique inputs can remain indefinitely.

title: Working authentication credential hardcoded in test source
description: The test source embeds a working account password and uses it to obtain authorization tokens. If test artifacts, source access, or a non-isolated test/staging deployment are exposed, an attacker can reuse the disclosed `jim@<application.domain>` / `ncc-1701` credential to authenticate and receive a bearer token. This is less certain as a production issue because the file is test code and the account may be fixture-only, but the credential is demonstrably accepted by the application instance created by this test.

trace.description: The test directly invokes the external `login` helper against the created Express application; the underlying authentication endpoint/helper implementation is outside this file.
A fixed account identity is constructed from the publicly configured application domain rather than supplied from an isolated secret store.

The fixed plaintext password `ncc-1701` is passed to `login`, which returns a bearer token later used successfully for an authenticated API request. Disclosure of this source value therefore supplies a reusable authentication credential wherever this account exists.

title: Hardcoded application and administrator credentials in test source
description: The test suite embeds reusable credentials for multiple application accounts, including the privileged `admin` account with password `admin123`. Any party able to read the source or distributed test artifacts obtains credentials that are submitted to the application's real login flow. The same pattern also exposes credentials for named user accounts elsewhere in the file. Although these may be fixture accounts, embedding static account passwords creates an authentication risk if the accounts or password values are present outside an isolated test environment.

The test hardcodes the administrator email and plaintext password `admin123`, then passes them to the login helper to obtain a bearer token. This exposes a privileged credential in source and uses it in an authentication decision.

title: Unauthenticated users can modify products through PUT /api/Products/:id
description: The test demonstrates that the privileged product-update function is reachable through the public API without an Authorization header. An unauthenticated caller can select the product identifier configured for the tampering challenge and successfully change its description. This is broken function-level access control: authentication is enforced for DELETE in adjacent tests, but PUT is deliberately accepted without authentication.

The request targets tamperingProductId and supplies a replacement product description in the JSON body.

The test asserts that the unauthenticated update completes with HTTP 200 and returns the modified product data, proving the function-level authorization check is absent or bypassable on this operation.

title: Public product update permits persistence of unsanitized HTML
description: The unauthenticated product-update path accepts and returns a description containing raw HTML without sanitization or encoding. Because product descriptions are persisted application content and are commonly rendered in product views, an attacker able to use this endpoint can store markup for later browser rendering. The visible payload is a benign anchor, but the test's exact equality assertion shows the API preserves markup verbatim; a script-capable HTML payload could therefore become stored XSS if the downstream product renderer does not contextually encode it. The rendering sink is outside this file.

trace.description: The test calls the public PUT /api/Products/:id route without an Authorization header; the externally facing handler and its persistence implementation are outside this file.
An attacker-controlled description containing HTML markup is supplied in the request body.

The test confirms a 200 response and that the returned description exactly equals the raw HTML input, demonstrating that this write path does not sanitize or encode the stored value. Any browser-rendering sink for product descriptions is outside this file.

title: Unbounded request-body buffering in network-exposed LLM mock
description: The test LLM mock binds an HTTP server on a fixed port and accumulates every incoming request body into a JavaScript string without a byte limit or early rejection. Node's HTTP parser does not impose an application body-size limit here. When this test server is running, a network client able to reach the listener can send a very large or indefinitely chunked POST request, causing the test process to consume memory until the request ends or the process becomes unstable. This is limited to the test/mock environment, but the listener is not explicitly restricted to loopback and no request-size control is present.

trace.description: The HTTP server callback receives an externally supplied IncomingMessage; the caller is outside this file and can provide an arbitrary request body while the mock server is running.
The server is started with only a port argument. No loopback host restriction, request-size limit, or application-level throttling is configured for the listener.

Each received body chunk is converted to text and concatenated into body without a maximum length before processing is deferred until the end event, making memory consumption proportional to attacker-supplied body size.

title: Unauthenticated registration permits caller-controlled administrator role
description: The integration test establishes that the publicly reachable user-registration API accepts a caller-supplied `role: 'admin'` and creates the account successfully without an authorization header. Role is a privilege-bearing property that must be assigned server-side or restricted to an authorized administrator. An unauthenticated attacker can register an administrator account and then use its elevated privileges. This is both mass assignment/property-level authorization failure and broken access control; it also reflects a trust-boundary design failure because the server accepts a client-selected authorization level.

The attacker-controlled JSON body supplies the privileged `role` property as `admin`, alongside registration credentials.
The successful 201 response and returned `role: 'admin'` assertion demonstrate that the API accepted and created the caller-selected administrator role rather than rejecting or server-overriding it.

title: User-controlled field projection exposes password property
description: The test demonstrates that the `fields` query parameter can select the password property from the authenticated user's API representation. Password hashes are sensitive authentication material and should never be selectable through a client-controlled projection. An authenticated account can request `fields=id,email,password` and receive its stored password value, enabling offline cracking attempts and exposing credential-derived data to browser clients, proxies, or any party able to access that account/session.

The requested projection explicitly includes the sensitive `password` model property.
The response contains a string-valued `user.password`, proving that the sensitive property is returned when selected by the client.

title: Feedback creation permits caller-controlled user impersonation
description: The tested API accepts a caller-supplied UserId when creating feedback, rather than deriving attribution from an authenticated identity or forbidding anonymous attribution. The test explicitly demonstrates that an unauthenticated caller can create feedback attributed to UserId 3, and that a logged-in caller can choose a different UserId. An attacker can obtain a CAPTCHA and submit feedback in another user's name, causing attribution and reputation/data-integrity abuse.

trace.description: The test acts as an external anonymous client and invokes the attacker-facing POST /api/Feedbacks endpoint; the endpoint implementation is outside this file.
The request body supplies UserId: 3 under complete client control, along with a valid CAPTCHA obtained by the client.
The test confirms the server creates the feedback (201) and returns UserId 3, proving that the supplied identity was accepted without an ownership/identity binding check.

title: CAPTCHA answer is exposed to the client that must solve it
description: The anti-automation CAPTCHA workflow exposes the CAPTCHA answer in the response to GET /rest/captcha, then accepts that exact value in a feedback-creation request. A script can therefore fetch both captchaId and answer programmatically and immediately submit arbitrary feedback, defeating the intended human-verification step and enabling feedback spam or bulk creation. This is visible in the test configuration; whether production deploys the same CAPTCHA response behavior is outside this file.

trace.description: The test, acting as an unauthenticated external client, requests a CAPTCHA from GET /rest/captcha; the endpoint implementation is outside this file.
The test reads both captchaId and the answer directly from the server response and places them in the subsequent POST body, showing no human-only solving step is required.
The server accepts the programmatically obtained CAPTCHA values and creates feedback with HTTP 201.

title: Feedback API exposes raw database constraint errors
description: Submitting a feedback record with a nonexistent UserId causes the API to return the raw SQLite foreign-key constraint error to the caller. This exposes internal database technology and schema/constraint details through an attacker-triggerable error path, rather than returning a generic validation error. Such diagnostics assist endpoint/schema reconnaissance and should be logged server-side while being mapped to a safe client response.

trace.description: The test invokes POST /api/Feedbacks as an external anonymous client; the route's error handling is outside this file.
The caller supplies the invalid foreign-key value UserId: 4711, which triggers the database error path.
The test verifies that the API response exposes the internal SQLite error string SQLITE_CONSTRAINT: FOREIGN KEY constraint failed.

title: Hardcoded account credential used to mint bearer token
description: The test embeds a usable email/password pair and supplies it to the authentication helper to obtain a bearer token. If this test account or its password is present in any reachable non-test deployment (for example, a seeded staging environment), anyone with repository or artifact access can authenticate as Jim and obtain that account's token. The file alone cannot establish that this credential is deployed outside the isolated test application, so impact is scoped accordingly.

The source embeds the account email and plaintext password rather than obtaining them from a test-only secret provider or runtime environment.
The embedded credential is passed to login(), whose returned token is used as a Bearer credential; reuse of this deployed credential would directly select Jim's authenticated identity.

title: Basket association remains caller-updatable after creation without BasketId
description: The test documents that a caller can create a BasketItem without a BasketId and subsequently set its BasketId through PUT, despite the same API rejecting BasketId changes for items initially created with a basket. BasketId controls which basket receives the item and is therefore a security-sensitive association. This creates an alternate update state where caller-controlled property assignment bypasses the stated noUpdate constraint. The test uses BasketId 3 but does not establish in this file whether basket 3 belongs to Jim; if it belongs to another account, this is a direct BOLA that lets Jim place an item into another user's basket.

trace.description: The test sends an externally shaped POST body to the BasketItems route without a BasketId; the route handler that receives this body is outside this file.
The test confirms the resulting BasketItem has no BasketId, establishing the state that bypasses the ordinary noUpdate constraint.
The test then sends caller-controlled BasketId 3 in a PUT to the created item's identifier; the handler and ownership validation are outside this file.

The asserted 200 response and returned BasketId 3 document that the API accepts the sensitive association change in this state. No ownership relationship between the authenticated user and BasketId 3 is verified in this file.

title: Authenticated test permits collection-wide basket-item retrieval without demonstrated ownership scope
description: This test explicitly expects an authenticated ordinary account to receive 200 from the collection-wide GET /api/BasketItems endpoint, while only unauthenticated access is denied. A collection endpoint named and exercised as 'GET all basket items' can expose other users' basket contents unless the handler scopes the query to the bearer identity. The response body and handler query are not available here, so it cannot be confirmed whether server-side filtering exists; this is a low-confidence BOLA exposure candidate that should be verified with two accounts.

The token is assembled into the Authorization header used for later API calls.
The test dispatches an authenticated GET to the all-BasketItems collection and asserts success; this file contains no user/basket scope in the request or assertion.

title: Unauthenticated security-question lookup reveals account existence
description: The integration test documents that an unauthenticated caller can submit an arbitrary email address to the account-recovery security-question endpoint and receives a question only when that account exists; unknown accounts receive an empty object. This creates an account-enumeration oracle and discloses recovery metadata for discovered accounts. An attacker can probe candidate email addresses, identify registered users from the response shape, and use the returned question to focus social-engineering or answer-guessing attempts. The actual route implementation is outside this file, but this test asserts the externally observable behavior as expected.

trace.description: The test invokes the externally reachable GET /rest/user/security-question route with an email query parameter. The route handler is outside this file, but this call demonstrates the attacker-controlled input contract.
For a known email address, the test expects a successful response rather than requiring authentication or an account-recovery anti-enumeration flow.

The asserted response contains a security-question value for the known account, whereas the adjacent unknown-email test expects an empty object (lines 82-87), establishing a distinguishable account-existence oracle and recovery-metadata disclosure.

title: Public endpoint exposes verbose Express and ORM error details
description: The test explicitly expects a missing email parameter on a public endpoint to produce an HTML 500 response containing the Express application identifier and a detailed ORM/database query-validation error. This indicates verbose error rendering is enabled for this path instead of returning a controlled client error. Unauthenticated attackers can trigger it with GET /rest/user/security-question and obtain internal framework and query details useful for reconnaissance. The setting/error handler is outside this test file, but the test codifies its exposed behavior.

trace.description: The test invokes the public security-question endpoint without the required email query parameter; the handler and its error configuration are outside this file.
The expected status is 500, showing malformed client input reaches server error handling rather than a controlled validation response.
The test expects an HTML response, consistent with Express's verbose error rendering being exposed on this API path.
The asserted response body includes the application/Express identifier and the internal `WHERE parameter "email" has invalid "undefined" value` ORM error, which is the information-disclosure sink.

title: Textbook RSA over a small alphabet permits trivial ciphertext reversal
description: The script treats RSA ciphertext as confidential even though it uses deterministic, unpadded textbook RSA on a tiny known plaintext alphabet (printable characters plus whitespace). Because the modulus and public exponent are embedded as public parameters, anyone can reproduce the character-to-ciphertext table and invert every ciphertext character by lookup; no RSA private key or factorization is required. The resulting plaintext is printed directly from the encrypted announcement file.

Using the public modulus and exponent, the script deterministically encrypts every possible plaintext character in the complete expected alphabet and stores a reverse ciphertext-to-character lookup table. This demonstrates that each encrypted character can be recovered from public information alone because no randomized padding is used.

Each ciphertext line is looked up in the public brute-force table and the recovered plaintext announcement is emitted. An attacker can perform the same operation on any ciphertext produced by this scheme.

title: Deterministic textbook RSA exposes every encrypted character
description: The script applies raw, deterministic RSA directly to each individual document character without OAEP or any randomized padding. Because the plaintext domain is tiny (characters), anyone holding announcement_encrypted.md and the public N/e values can encrypt every candidate character with pow(ord(candidate), e, N) and match the resulting integer to each output line. This recovers the confidential document without factoring RSA or obtaining a private key. The 1024-bit modulus is also below current RSA deployment recommendations, but the per-character textbook-RSA construction is already an immediate confidentiality failure.

trace.description: The script opens the confidential document as input; its content is the sensitive plaintext entering this encryption routine from the local file source.
The entire confidential document is read and iterated character-by-character, restricting each RSA plaintext operation to a readily enumerable character value.
The RSA public modulus and exponent are defined as public parameters; they are sufficient for an attacker to generate the same deterministic ciphertext for each candidate character.

Each character is encrypted with raw modular exponentiation and written directly. No randomized padding (such as RSA-OAEP) is applied, so ciphertext equality reveals the character through an offline candidate-encryption lookup.

title: Prototype properties bypass country-mapping completeness validation
description: The completeness check uses the prototype-inclusive `in` operator rather than checking that `countryMapping` owns the challenge key. A challenge key such as `toString`, `constructor`, or `__proto__` is considered mapped through `Object.prototype` even when no corresponding mapping exists in `fbctf.yml`. Consequently, a malformed or compromised challenge-data update can pass this integrity test while omitting the required country mapping.

Challenge YAML is parsed into a JavaScript value and returned without schema validation of challenge keys.
The test extracts each parsed challenge `key` for use as the lookup key in the completeness check.
`key in countryMapping` succeeds for inherited prototype properties, not only actual country-mapping entries. The assertion therefore accepts prototype-named challenge keys with no own mapping.

title: Special country-code values evade uniqueness validation
description: The uniqueness test accumulates country codes in a normal `{}` object. A mapping code of `__proto__` invokes the inherited prototype setter instead of creating an own counter property; subsequent incrementing also does not produce an enumerable own counter. Since the final validation iterates only `Object.keys(countryCodeCounts)`, duplicated `__proto__` codes are omitted and the uniqueness assertion is never evaluated for them. The test therefore does not reliably enforce its stated mapping-integrity invariant for special property names.
