The YAML contents are parsed and later selected as `ctf.countryMapping` without validating that mapping codes are safe object-key values.
The parsed country mapping is assigned to `countryMapping`; its `code` fields remain unconstrained (`any`).
Each unvalidated `code` is used as a property name on a plain object. For `__proto__`, the assignment targets inherited prototype behavior rather than establishing the counter expected by the test.
The final assertion only processes enumerable own keys from `countryCodeCounts`; a `__proto__` counter is absent from that list, so duplicate values are skipped rather than rejected.

title: RSA private key exponent hardcoded in source
description: The RSA private exponent is embedded directly in source code. Anyone who can read this repository or an included copy of this script obtains the private key material and can decrypt ciphertexts protected by this RSA key; if the key is reused for signing or identity operations, they can also impersonate the key holder. Source-controlled private key material is both a cryptographic failure and a security misconfiguration.

trace.description: The script declares the RSA private exponent `d` as a source-code constant, exposing the secret to every party with access to this file or its distributed artifacts.
The exposed private exponent is supplied to `pow` together with the public modulus, performing the private-key RSA operation to recover plaintext from each ciphertext value.

title: Unauthenticated textbook RSA decryption of file-supplied ciphertext
description: The script performs raw RSA modular exponentiation directly on attacker-modifiable ciphertext integers read from a file. There is no OAEP/PSS-style padding validation or authenticated-encryption integrity check before decrypted bytes are emitted. Raw RSA is malleable: a party able to modify ciphertext can transform it into related plaintext on decryption, and malformed ciphertext receives no cryptographic authenticity rejection. The fixed file path limits demonstrated remote reachability, but the cryptographic construction itself is unauthenticated.

trace.description: The script receives ciphertext from `announcement_encrypted.md`; control of this file's contents is outside the script and no authenticity check is made when it is opened.
Each input line is converted directly to an arbitrary integer ciphertext value without validation of a signed or authenticated envelope.
`pow(int(f[:-1]), d, N)` applies raw RSA private-key exponentiation and immediately converts the result to output bytes, with no OAEP padding or integrity/authentication verification.

title: Unbounded ciphertext file processing with expensive RSA operations
description: The whole encrypted file is loaded with `readlines()` and every line triggers a costly large-integer modular exponentiation. There is no input-size, line-count, or rate limit. If an attacker can replace or influence `announcement_encrypted.md` and cause this script to run, a very large file causes excessive memory allocation and CPU work, potentially blocking the process. The file does not establish whether such control or repeated execution is attacker reachable.

trace.description: The script accepts all content from the fixed ciphertext file when it is opened; whether an external caller can control this file is not shown in this source file.
`readlines()` loads the complete file into memory before any processing, with no maximum size or line-count enforcement.
The list comprehension performs a large RSA modular exponentiation for every input line, making attacker-inflated input consume CPU in addition to memory.

title: Release artifacts use collision-broken MD5 integrity checksums
description: The packaging workflow publishes MD5 digest files as the artifact checksum. MD5 is collision-broken and does not provide a trustworthy integrity guarantee: an attacker able to substitute a distribution artifact can construct a different artifact with the same MD5 digest, defeating consumers that rely on the generated .md5 file for verification. Use a collision-resistant digest such as SHA-256 or, preferably, signed release artifacts.

trace.description: The externally invoked Grunt `checksum` task is the entrypoint; its caller is outside this file and causes every file in `dist/` to be processed as a release artifact.
The task reads each distribution artifact and feeds its full contents into the selected digest algorithm.
The integrity mechanism explicitly instantiates the deprecated, collision-broken `md5` hash and subsequently writes its digest as the artifact checksum.

title: Distribution archive includes key material paths
description: The distributable package explicitly includes `ctf.key` and the complete `encryptionkeys/` directory. If these paths contain operational private keys, symmetric keys, or signing material—as their names indicate—any recipient of the archive can extract them and impersonate protected operations or decrypt protected data. This file does not establish whether the files are deliberately public challenge fixtures versus production key material, so that must be verified; nevertheless, packaging key-named files into a broadly distributed archive is an unsafe release configuration.

trace.description: The externally invoked `package` task is the entrypoint; its caller is outside this file and runs the archive-generation configuration.
The `compress:pckg` configuration defines the file set that will be copied into the release archive.
The archive explicitly includes the file named `ctf.key`, exposing it to every archive recipient.
The archive also includes every file under `encryptionkeys/`; no exclusion, environment gate, or key-redaction control is present in this packaging rule.

title: Plaintext reusable test-account password is committed to source
description: The test source embeds a reusable account email pattern and plaintext password, then uses them to obtain a valid authentication token from the initialized application. If this test account is present in any deployed or accessible non-isolated environment, disclosure of the repository gives an attacker known credentials. Test fixtures should use ephemeral credentials created at runtime, and test users must be excluded or randomized outside isolated test environments.

trace.description: The test invokes the external authentication helper to authenticate against the initialized application; the helper implementation and authentication endpoint are outside this file.
The account identity is derived from configured application domain data, making this a concrete account rather than a generated one-time test identity.
A plaintext password literal, "ncc-1701", is supplied to the login operation, placing a credential directly in committed source and using it to establish an authenticated session.

title: Profile image URL workflow permits loopback-target SSRF
description: The URL-based profile-image workflow is specified to accept a caller-controlled URL pointing to localhost and to retrieve/write the successful response as the user profile image. This demonstrates that the endpoint does not reject loopback destinations. An authenticated attacker can substitute 127.0.0.1, localhost, private-network hosts, or cloud metadata addresses for imageUrl, causing the application to issue requests from its trusted network position. Returned content may be persisted as a profile image, potentially enabling blind probing or exfiltration where the response is made accessible.

trace.description: The POST /profile/image/url request is the attacker-facing route exercised by this test; its handler is outside this file.
Caller-controlled imageUrl is populated with an http URL whose host is localhost and whose port is dynamically chosen by the local listener.

The valid-response test specifies that the route processes the URL response by writing the file and redirecting. This is evidence that the route performs the outbound retrieval of the unvalidated loopback destination; the actual HTTP-client call is in the route implementation outside this test file.

title: Invalid upload exposes framework-branded error details
description: For an invalid profile-image upload, the application returns an HTML error response that exposes both the application/framework banner (including Express) and an internal error message. The test asserts this externally visible behavior, so it is not merely an unobserved possibility. Detailed framework-branded errors assist fingerprinting and can disclose increasingly sensitive implementation details when other upload/parser failures occur; production error handling should return a generic client error while logging diagnostic details server-side.

trace.description: The test sends an externally reachable POST request to the profile image upload route; the production route handler is outside this file.
An invalid DOCX file is supplied in the multipart file field, driving the route's error path.
The test verifies that the externally returned HTML contains the application name and the Express framework banner, demonstrating production-visible diagnostic/framework disclosure.

title: Unauthenticated LLM tool can issue arbitrary coupons without server-side eligibility enforcement
description: The unauthenticated chat agent exposes a coupon-generation capability, but the server-side tool enforces none of the stated eligibility controls. Any caller can supply chat messages intended to cause the model to invoke generateCoupon; the tool neither requires a logged-in customer nor verifies an order, damaged-order status, rejected return/exchange, one-time issuance, or the maximum discount. In fact, the system prompt itself contains a confidential instruction to offer a 15% courtesy discount on a customer-controlled complaint/escalation scenario, while the tool accepts any numeric discount. Prompt instructions are not an authorization control, so an attacker can obtain discount codes or potentially arbitrary discount values by directing the model to call the tool. Coupon issuance is also only counted as an aggregate metric and is not auditable to a customer, request, eligibility evidence, or issued code.

trace.description: The exported chat handler receives an externally supplied request. Its caller is outside this file; architecture context shows POST /rest/chat has no authentication middleware.
Caller-controlled messages are accepted directly from the request body, with no authentication or authorization requirement before they are provided to the agent.
The messages and all chat tools are supplied to streamText, allowing model-directed tool invocation based on attacker-controlled conversation content.

generateCoupon calls security.generateCoupon with the model-selected discount and returns the usable code. It performs no customer authentication, order lookup, damaged-order/return validation, discount maximum check, issuance limit, or security audit log.

title: Unauthenticated chat endpoint permits unbounded LLM and streaming resource consumption
description: POST /rest/chat is an unauthenticated, externally backed streaming LLM endpoint with no rate limit, request/message-size cap, concurrency limit, or output-token limit visible in this handler. An attacker can submit large message histories and issue many concurrent requests, consuming LLM context processing, generated-token capacity, open SSE connections, and potentially tool/database work. stopWhen(stepCountIs(10)) limits agent steps only; it does not limit incoming context size, model output per step, request frequency, or concurrent streams. Aggregate metrics record consumption after the fact but do not prevent exhaustion.

trace.description: The exported handler receives externally supplied POST /rest/chat requests; the route is registered without authentication middleware according to the supplied architecture context.
The handler accepts req.body.messages without validating its size, number of messages, or aggregate token budget.
The only visible agent bound is a ten-step stop condition. This does not impose a request rate, connection/concurrency, input-token, or output-token limit.
streamText submits attacker-influenced messages to the configured remote LLM and opens a streamed result that is consumed until completion, creating an expensive per-request resource sink.

title: Order ownership check trusts JWT identity obtained by decode rather than visible verification
description: Order authorization derives the current user identity by decoding the presented JWT, but this file contains no signature verification, expiration validation, or authenticated middleware before using the decoded id. If security.decode is a non-verifying JWT decode operation, as its use and name imply, an attacker can alter or forge the token payload's data.id to select a victim account. The subsequent ownership check then uses the victim account's email, so it incorrectly authorizes an order belonging to that victim and returns it through the chat tool. The implementation of security.decode is outside this file, so whether it independently verifies signatures cannot be conclusively established here.

trace.description: The chat handler receives an external request and can invoke getOrderById from the public chat route; the route has no authentication middleware in the supplied routing context.
getUserId extracts a JWT and passes it to security.decode, then trusts decoded.data.id. No signature, issuer, expiry, or audience verification is performed anywhere in this visible function.
The decoded id is used to retrieve the selected user's email, establishing the identity used for the later ownership decision.
The tool retrieves an arbitrary requested order identifier from the orders collection.

The ownership comparison is against the email for the identity selected from the decoded token, and a match returns the complete order. A forged decoded id therefore makes this check evaluate as the victim's authorization check.

title: Hardcoded cookie-signing secret enables signed-cookie forgery
description: The application configures cookie-parser with the literal signing secret "kekse". Any cookie signature produced with this secret can be reproduced by an attacker who can inspect the source or otherwise learns this well-known value. If signed cookies are used by this application or middleware to carry security-relevant state, the attacker can forge otherwise trusted signed-cookie values. Hardcoded cryptographic secrets are also a deployment/configuration integrity failure regardless of current use.

trace.description: Inbound HTTP requests, including attacker-controlled Cookie headers, are processed by the globally installed cookie parser.
cookieParser is initialized with the source-code literal "kekse" as its signing secret, rather than a protected, deployment-specific secret.

title: Login endpoint permits unlimited credential-guessing attempts
description: The login endpoint is registered without any rate-limiting middleware, unlike reset-password and 2FA operations elsewhere in this file. An attacker can submit unlimited credential guesses to /rest/user/login, consuming authentication/database resources and enabling online password brute force or credential stuffing. The absence of a limiter is directly material to the authentication decision made by the external login handler.

trace.description: An unauthenticated attacker can repeatedly POST credentials to the /rest/user/login entrypoint.
The route dispatches every request directly to login() with no rateLimit middleware or other throttle registered on this route, allowing unbounded authentication attempts.

title: Reset-password rate limit is bypassable through X-Forwarded-For spoofing
description: The reset-password rate limiter keys clients using the caller-supplied X-Forwarded-For header whenever present. The app globally enables Express trust proxy, so this deployment trusts forwarded-address information rather than constraining it to a known proxy configuration. A direct attacker can vary X-Forwarded-For on each request and receive a fresh rate-limit bucket, bypassing the 100-attempt reset-password restriction. This permits excessive reset attempts and undermines the authentication/account-recovery control.

trace.description: An unauthenticated client reaches the password-reset route protected by the intended five-minute, 100-request limiter.
The application globally enables trust proxy without limiting trusted proxy addresses, increasing reliance on forwarded client-address headers.
The limiter takes an attacker-controlled X-Forwarded-For header as its key whenever supplied; changing that header evades the per-key limit and allows repeated reset/authentication attacks.

title: Generated user registration permits mass assignment of unexcluded privilege fields
description: The generated User REST resource is configured as automatic CRUD with an exclusion list containing only password and totpSecret. The public registration route only checks/normalizes email and password fields and does not remove or server-derive authorization-sensitive properties. In particular, the generated resource's model attributes beyond those two exclusions, such as a User role/privilege property, remain caller bindable. An unauthenticated requester can submit an extra privilege field (for example, role=admin) during registration and have the generated create endpoint persist it, resulting in privilege escalation.

trace.description: Unauthenticated callers POST a registration body to /api/Users; this middleware validates only email/password/passwordRepeat and leaves other body properties intact.

The User automatic-resource configuration excludes only password and totpSecret, establishing a deny-list rather than an explicit writable-property allow-list; privilege-related User attributes are not excluded here.
finale.resource creates the generated /api/Users CRUD endpoint backed by UserModel, automatically binding request properties to the model and persisting the submitted User record.

title: Unauthenticated encryption-key directory enumeration and file serving
description: The application publicly exposes both an index of the encryptionkeys directory and a handler for individual files below it. No authentication/authorization middleware is registered for either path. An attacker can enumerate the directory and request discovered key files, potentially obtaining cryptographic material that should never be web-accessible; possession of such keys can compromise encrypted content or signatures that rely on them.

trace.description: An unauthenticated attacker requests /encryptionkeys and obtains the directory-browsing response.
serve-index is mounted directly on the encryptionkeys filesystem directory and exposes discoverable file names without an access-control middleware.
After identifying a file name, the attacker requests /encryptionkeys/:file, which is dispatched to the key-file serving handler with no authorization guard in this registration.

title: Support-log directory and log files are publicly exposed
description: Support logs are exposed through an unauthenticated directory-index mount and a file-serving route. The intervening verify.accessControlChallenges middleware is challenge instrumentation, and the supplied route metadata identifies these mounts as carrying no authentication or authorization middleware. Attackers can enumerate log names and retrieve logs that commonly contain request URLs, source IPs, identifiers, error details, and operational information, undermining the confidentiality of security logging.

trace.description: An unauthenticated attacker requests /support/logs to access the log directory.
serve-index is mounted over the logs directory before the challenge-verification middleware, making directory browsing externally reachable.
The /support/logs/:file route serves a selected log file through serveLogFiles() without an authorization middleware on the registration.

title: Public generated API collections have pagination disabled
description: The finale-generated REST resources explicitly disable pagination. At least the Recycles list endpoint is exposed without an authentication middleware and proceeds to generated CRUD handling after its challenge middleware. A requester can repeatedly request the full resource collection, forcing the server/database to build and serialize every Recycle record in one response. As record volume grows, this becomes an unauthenticated memory, CPU, database, and bandwidth exhaustion vector.

trace.description: An unauthenticated caller can request GET /api/Recycles; the route has no authorization middleware and only runs the recycle challenge middleware.
finale generates resource endpoints including /api/Recycles and /api/Recycles/:id backed by the Recycle model.
The generated resource is configured with pagination: false, so list requests are not bounded by a server-side page size.

title: Development diagnostic error handler is enabled unconditionally
description: The production application unconditionally installs the errorhandler package as its final error handler. There is no environment gate restricting it to development. errorhandler generates diagnostic error responses, including stack/error details, for unhandled application errors; an attacker can trigger malformed or exceptional requests and obtain internal implementation information useful for follow-on attacks.

trace.description: Any external request that causes an unhandled error in a preceding route or middleware reaches the global Express error chain; the originating handler is outside this file.
errorhandler() is installed without any production-environment condition, exposing its diagnostic error-response behavior to requests that trigger errors.
